units.la: Inter Prophetas veteres illustris merito censendus est Daniel. Hic certe Prophetae nomen & omen habet. Nomine Prophetae ipsum dignatus est Christus Matth. xxiv. 15. nec non Josephus, qui ipsum appellat ἕνα τῶν μεγίστων θεοφητῶν Ant. Lib. x. Cap. xii. Neque omine ipso destituitur. Possem adducere, quod Propheta vocetur, qui Deo familiaris ac singulariter acceptus est Genef. xx. 7. Pfal. cv. 14. 15, qui frequenter calidas simul ac validas apud Deum preces fundit Gen. xx. 7. cujus labia laudem ac gloriam Dei celebrant 1 Sam. x. 5. 1 Chron. xxv. 1. 2. 3. &c. sicuti haec omnia in Daniele Daniele inveniuntur, qui אִישׁ חֲמֻדוֹת Vir Desideriorum Dei, h. e. Deo desiderabilis, placens ac carum caput Dan. ix. 23. x. 19. hinc etiam Noacho & Jobo comparandus Ezech. xiv. 14. 20. quique in laudibus divinis & in precibus frequens ac apud Deum validus erat, tanto certe excellentior inter Prophetas, quanto frequentior ac validior in precibus Dan. ii. 19. vi. 11. ix. 3. Sed magis speciatim spectato, & quae ad Prophetam proprie dictum pertinent. Sic utique Propheta erat, cui res arcanas vel praesentes vel praeteritas vel futuras revelabat Deus, maxime in insomniis ac visionibus Numer. xii. 6. Porro qui a Deo acceptas revelationes eloquitur ac cum aliis communicat Jer. xxiii. 22. 28. atque sic Ecclesiam docet instruitque de consilio ejus voce vel scripto; quo pertinet illud de Aharone, qui Propheta Moses dicitur, quia ex ipsius ore, quasi Dei sui verba accepta elocuturus erat, perinde ac Prophetae Dei a Deo accepta eloquuntur verba Exod. vii. 1. coll. Exod. iv. 15. Denique qui dies Messiae ac mysteria regni ejus annunciat, Testimonium enim Jesu est spiritus Prophetiae Apoc. xix. 10. unde merito illi Prophetae, qui Christo testimonium dant Act. x. 43. 1 Pet. i. 11. Tandem qui non ad tempus & semel forte revelationes accepit, sed saepius, ac apud quem per multos annos Prophetia permanet. Ex his omnibus facile colligi potest, quod Daniel habendus sit inter excellentissimos ac proprie dictos Prophetas. Quod liquet sive arcanorum revelationes & futurorum declarationes etiam in insomniis ac visionibus mirandis ipsi factas respiciamus, sive scripta ejus adhucdum extantia, quibus revelata sibi communicat ac Ecclesiam docet, intueamur, sive oracula de Messia ejusque regno illustrissima cogitemus Cap. ii. 44. 45. vii. 13. 14. ix. 24. &c. sive denique revelationum frequentiam ac prophetiae permanentiam apud ipsum ad seram usque aetatem consideremus. Quapropter merito rejicienda crisis Judaeorum est, qui ut elevent hujus viri Prophetias ac Christi de ipso elogium enervent, eum choro Prophetarum ejicere studeant, hac in parte a Christianis quibusdam neutiquam sequendi. Talia enim proferunt Prophetae γνωρίσματα, quae aperte Scripturis contraria affectatam fingendi libidinem in ipsis ostendunt. Qualia sunt, prophetiam non cadere super captivum, exulem, tristem, decrepitum senem &c. quae exemplis Jeremiae
units.tr: Among the ancient prophets, Daniel deservedly counts as one of the most illustrious. Certainly the name Prophet is both his name and his omen. Christ himself deigned to give him the name of prophet (Matt. 24:15), and so did Josephus, who calls him "one of the greatest theoprophets" [ἕνα τῶν μεγίστων θεοφητῶν] (Antiquities, book 10, chapter 12). Nor is he without the omen itself. I could cite that he is called a prophet who was familiar with God and singularly acceptable to him (Gen. 20:7; Ps. 105:14-15), who often pours out prayers that are both fervent and powerful before God (Gen. 20:7), whose lips celebrate the praise and glory of God (1 Sam. 10:5; 1 Chron. 25:1-3, etc.). All these things are found in Daniel, who is a man of desires [אִישׁ חֲמֻדוֹת], that is, desirable to God, pleasing and dear to him (Dan. 9:23; 10:19). Hence he is also to be compared with Noah and Job (Ezek. 14:14, 20). He was frequent in the praises of God and in prayer, and powerful with God, and so he was far more excellent among the prophets, as he was more frequent and more powerful in prayers (Dan. 2:19; 6:11; 9:3). But let us look more specifically at what pertains to a Prophet properly so called. He was a prophet to whom God revealed hidden things, whether present, past or future, above all in dreams and visions (Num. 12:6). A prophet is also one who speaks the revelations received from God and communicates them to others (Jer. 23:22, 28), and so teaches and instructs the Church about God's counsel, by voice or in writing. To this belongs what is said of Aaron, who is called a prophet of Moses, because he was to speak from Moses' mouth as if they were the words of his God, just as the prophets of God speak the words received from God (Exod. 7:1; compare Exod. 4:15). Finally, a prophet is one who announces the days of the Messiah and the mysteries of his kingdom, "for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy" (Rev. 19:10). Whence those prophets are rightly so called who bear witness to Christ (Acts 10:43; 1 Pet. 1:11). Lastly, a prophet is one who has received revelations not once and by chance, but often, and in whom prophecy remains over many years. From all this it can easily be gathered that Daniel is to be regarded as among the most excellent and properly so-called prophets. This is clear whether we look at the revelations of hidden things and the declarations of future things made to him even in dreams and wonderful visions; or whether we look at his writings still extant, in which he communicates what has been revealed to him and teaches the Church; or whether we consider the most illustrious oracles about the Messiah and his kingdom (Dan. 2:44-45; 7:13-14; 9:24, etc.); or finally whether we consider the frequency of his revelations and the permanence of prophecy in him right down to a late age. Therefore the criticism of the Jews is rightly rejected. They strive to expel this man from the choir of prophets, in order to lower his prophecies and weaken Christ's testimony about him. In this respect they are by no means to be followed by certain Christians. For they put forward the marks of prophets [γνωρίσματα], which openly show a contrived lust for invention, contrary to the Scriptures. Such marks are: that prophecy does not fall upon a captive, an exile, a sad man, a decrepit old man, and so on, which are refuted by the examples of Jeremiah

Ratio vera, ob quam recutiti Danielem Prophetis annumerare nolunt, est occulta, scilicet quia nimis illustria sunt Viri hujus vaticinia, præsertim illud quod præ manibus habemus, & per manifestam hujus prophetiæ lucem ne volentibus quidem cæcutire tenebrarum filiis licet.

They distinguish in particular between the first and the second degree of prophecy, calling the one nebuah [נבואה] and the other ruach hakodesh [רוח הקדש]. But one must marvel at their blindness, in that they assign the Holy Spirit as a second degree of prophecy to the one who receives revelation by the hidden impulse of the Spirit with his senses intact, and prophecy to the one who, with the use of his senses taken away, whether waking or sleeping, sees visions or hears a voice speaking to him. They do not assign prophecy to Daniel but the Holy Spirit as a second degree, since it is established that his mind, after the first presentation of divine things, was so often overwhelmed and dismayed by such a blaze of majesty that his body, drained of strength, lay without motion or sense (Dan. 8:17-18, 27; 10:8). Nor does the argument which Kimchi uses in his preface to the Psalms hold, that "his virtue and knowledge did not attain to those visions, according to the virtue of Isaiah, Ezekiel and the other prophets." For that is said without warrant, since he received the visions together with their interpretations and ascribed to himself the understanding of the vision (ch. 10:1). Certainly he surpassed many in wisdom and in the understanding of hidden things (Ezek. 28:3). As for the order of the Bible, where Daniel is placed among the Writings, this is not the same in all copies, and therefore he is neither considered divine nor approved by Christ (Luke 24:44). Christ seems rather to look to the division of books which Josephus gives in book 1 against Apion, where he mentions the Law in five books, the Prophets from Moses to Artaxerxes, Daniel included, in thirteen books, and hymns in four books. The true reason why the Jews are unwilling to count Daniel among the Prophets is hidden: namely, that the prophecies of this man are too illustrious, especially the one we have before us. By the manifest light of this prophecy, not even the sons of darkness, though they wish it, are permitted to be blinded.

units.la: II. Certe hæc nostra Prophetia, in qua Messiæ persona, status, munera, beneficia, judicia, cum temporis determinatione, quo omnia eventura erant, clarè describuntur, onus illud Judæis est, quod excutere non valent, adeò ut eam non extare, saltem non legi vellent, perdita cæterum impudentia depravare sustinentes mentem ejus pro obduratione cordis eorum. Uti verò desideramus restitutionem gentis illius ac conversionem versionem ad Messiam suum, dudum natum passum & exalta-tum, ita certè dignius argumentum vix inveniri potest in quo occupemur, & ubi majori spe opera nostra collocetur, quam in explicandis ac vindicandis vaticiniis antiquis, quibus Mes-sias noster vivis coloribus depictus atque delineatus fuit. Un-de etiam nos operam nostram haud perdidisse rati in elucidatio-ne horum verborum qualicunque, eadem selegimus, ut sint mate-ries excercitationis hujus, cogitantes vix quemquam Prophetarum fuisse, qui studiis nostris adeò commendatus legitur in sacris & à Christo ipso, ac Daniel, imo hic ipse locus noster.
units.tr: II. Certainly this our prophecy, in which the person, state, offices, benefits and judgments of the Messiah are clearly described, together with the determination of the time when all these things were to come to pass, is a burden the Jews cannot throw off. So much so that they would wish it did not exist, or at least were not read, and with shameless depravity they undertake to distort its meaning in place of the hardness of their own hearts. Just as we desire the restoration of that nation and its conversion to its Messiah, who was long since born, suffered and was exalted, so indeed a more worthy subject can hardly be found in which to occupy ourselves, nor one in which our labour may be placed with greater hope, than the explanation and vindication of the ancient prophecies by which our Messiah was depicted and outlined in vivid colours. Hence we too, thinking that our labour would not be lost in the elucidation, however slight, of these words, have chosen them as the matter of this exercise, reflecting that hardly any of the prophets is so commended to our studies in the sacred writings, and by Christ himself, as Daniel, and indeed this very passage of ours.

units.la: III. Dignissimam ergò materiam ut ordine tractemus, non solum sensum verborum indagabimus, sed & eorum veritatem de monstrabimus. Ut verò verborum mens clarius constet non inutile erit occasionem eorum & scopum ex antecedentibus aliquantulum illustrare. Nempe Daniel anno primo Darii Medi ex Prophetiis Jeremiæ, quæ extant Jerem. xxv. 11. xxix. 10. annos Captivitatis Babylonicæ à Deo definitos esse septua-ginta, atque adeò finem illius jam instare, edoctus, ad preces confugit, etiam à Jeremiâ præscriptas Jer. xxix. 12. 13, suo sic exemplo docens certitudinem consilii ac prædictionis divinæ cum precibus, ut mediis divinitus ordinatis, neutiquam pug-nare. Petit verò vir sanctissimus populi sui urbisque ac sanc-tuarii restitutionem, & quidem propter fines decentissimos; quorum ultimus est gloria Dei. Domine exaudi, Domine condo-na, Domine attende, & effice, ne tardato למענך אלהי propter te ipsum Deus mi verf. 19. subordinatus vero sponsionis æternæ factæ à Filio Redemtore exsolutio, atque adeo Messiæ apparitio in carne, in terrâ Canaanis ac inter populum suum. Hoc intendit Daniel verf. 17. Ausculta Deus noster orationi servitui, & propter Dominum למען ארני. Ubi nulla necessitas nos cogit, ut dicamus hic nomen positum pro pronomine, sensus enim emphaticus ac fidei patrum convenientissimus emer-git, conf. Psalm. lxxx. 15. quem etiam responsum, quod at-tulit Gabriel de populo reducendo & civitate restauranda prop-ter Messiam & opera gratiæ ab ipso perficienda, efflagitare vi-detur. Propter Dominum ergò cum dicat Daniel, non solum propter sponsionem Filii & hac nixam ejus intercessionem apud Patrem, de qua Job xxxiii. 23. 24. sed & propter eum olim ex gente Israelitica oriundum, ac in medio ipsius terrae-que Canaanis habitaturum, à Deo exaudiri petit, non subsi-stens in externa populi liberatione, sed hanc unice desiderans propter Messiam. Oratio haec viri Deo chari etiam fructu suo haud caruit. Etenim adhuc loquenti, oranti, ac peccata confitenti apparuit illico coelestis nuncius, ipsi precum suarum gratiosam exauditionem nunciaturus, ac hoc pacto sollicitum Vatem consolaturus. Declarat nempe Gabriel, populum esse reducendum, ac civitatem sanctam restaurandam, & quidem propter Messiam & peccatorum expiationem, justitiaeque aeternae adductionem per ipsum futuram. Hunc idcirco venturum ad suos, idque in fine LXX. septimanarum, postquam Deus gra-vitatem irae suae in captivitate LXX. annorum, renovato favore gratia ac longanimitate in populum Judaicum septuplo longio-ri temporis spatio compensaret. Unde apparet Angelum in his-ce gentis Judaicae calamitates continuandas non denunciare, uti-vellent Judaei contra scopum & contextum.
units.tr: III. Therefore, to treat this most worthy matter in order, we shall not only investigate the sense of the words but also demonstrate their truth. So that the meaning of the words may be clearer, it will not be useless to explain a little the occasion and the purpose from what precedes. Namely, Daniel, in the first year of Darius the Mede, having learned from the prophecies of Jeremiah (Jer. 25:11; 29:10) that the seventy years of the Babylonian captivity fixed by God were complete and that its end was now at hand, took refuge in prayer, which Jeremiah had also prescribed (Jer. 29:12-13). Thus by his example he taught that the certainty of God's counsel and prediction does not conflict with prayers as divinely ordained means. The most holy man asks for the restoration of his people, city and sanctuary, and indeed for the most fitting ends, of which the last is the glory of God. "O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive; O Lord, attend and act, and do not delay, for your own sake, my God" (v. 19). Subordinate to this is the fulfilment of the eternal promise made by the Son as Redeemer, and thus the appearance of the Messiah in the flesh, in the land of Canaan and among his people. Daniel intends this in verse 17: "Hear, our God, the prayer of your servant," and "for the Lord's sake" [למען ארני]. Here no necessity compels us to say that the name is put for the pronoun. The emphatic sense, and that most agreeable to the faith of the fathers, emerges (compare Ps. 80:15), which he also seems to demand in the answer brought by Gabriel about the restoration of the people and the rebuilding of the city for the sake of the Messiah and the works of grace to be accomplished by him. Therefore, since Daniel says "for the Lord's sake," he asks to be heard by God not only for the sake of the Son's promise and his intercession resting on it before the Father (Job 33:23-24), but also for the sake of him who was to be born in time past from the Israelite nation and to dwell in the midst of that very land of Canaan. He does not rest in the external deliverance of the people, but desires this solely for the sake of the Messiah. This prayer of the man dear to God did not lack its fruit. For while he was still speaking, praying and confessing sins, at once a heavenly messenger appeared, to announce to him the gracious answer to his prayers and so console the anxious seer. Gabriel declares, namely, that the people is to be brought back and the holy city restored, and indeed for the sake of the Messiah, and for the expiation of sins and the bringing in of eternal righteousness to be effected through him. He is therefore to come to his own, and that at the end of the seventy weeks, after God, having satisfied the severity of his wrath in the seventy years of captivity, would with renewed favour, grace and long-suffering toward the Jewish people make amends over a span of time seven times longer. Whence it appears that the angel does not announce that the calamities of the Jewish nation are to continue, as the Jews would wish, contrary to the scope and context.

units.la: IV. Generatim determinat Angelus tempus longanimitatis ac gratiae Dei super populum Danielis, propter opera Mes-siae intra illud temporis spatium ad salutem electorum pe-ragenda vers. 24. In temporis generali notatione occurrunt non solum summa ejus definita, sed & objectum, cui istius tempo-ris duratio tribuitur, quin etiam fines decentissimi, ob quos hoc tempus à Deo genti Danielis datum est.
units.tr: IV. In general the angel fixes the period of God's longsuffering and grace towards the people of Daniel, on account of the work of the Messiah to be accomplished within that span of time for the salvation of the elect (ver. 24). In the general statement of the period there occur not only its definite total, but also its object, to which the duration of that period is assigned, and indeed also the most fitting ends for which this period was given by God to the people of Daniel.

units.la: V. Temporis universi summa sancta quâdam styli sublimi-tate proponitur, cum non per annos, sed per septimanas illud numerat Angelus [Hebrew] apud LXX. [Greek] Vulg. Septuaginta hebdomades abbreviatae sunt. Notat vulgò septimana, Hebraeis [Hebrew] & [Hebrew] spatium septem dierum in orbem continuò redeuntium, & illa ad distinctionem ab alius generis septimanis dicitur septimana dierum. Sic testatur Daniel, quod fuerit in luctu atque jejunio tres [Hebrew] septimanas dierum Dan. x. 2. 3. Quandoque vero notat in sacris spatium septem annorum, singulis diebus pro totidem annis positis, uti id frequenter usu venit Ezech. iv. 6. Apoc. xii. 6. &c. Atque huc trahunt quidam illud Labanis ad Jacobum [Hebrew] / Imple septimanam istam i. e. septennium istud, & dabimus tibi etiam il-lam. {*}lam pro servitute, quâ servies apud me adhuc septem annos alios. Gen. xxxix. 27. Ubi praestat forte ואת referre ad Leam, ac septimanam nuptiis ejus destinatam intelligere, conf: Gen. z. 10. Jud. xiv. 14. Tob xi. 20. Ab aliis huc refertur illud Jeremiae cap. v. 24. ubi Deus exprobrans summam Judaeis ingratitudinem, dicit illos ad animum non revocare, quod dederit ipsis pluviam tempestivam ac serotinam tempore suo, & quod servaverit ipsis שבעוה חקוה קציר. Extra omne vero dubium est positus locus Levit. xxv. 8. Et numerabis tibi שבע שבתוח שנים septem septimanas annorum, septem annos, septem vicibus, & erunt tibi ימי שבתות השניים dies septimanarum annorum quadraginta novem anni. Similis locutionis exemplum produxit A. Gellius Noct. Att. Lib. iii. Cap. x. ex M. Varrone, qui alicubi testatur se quoque jam duodecimam annorum hebdomadam ingressum esse, ridiculè adjiciens, se ad eum diem septuaginta hebdomadas librorum conscripsisse. Similiter loquitur Macrobius Lib. v. 5. Cap. vi. in Somnium Scipion. Et quarta annorum hebdomas impleta in latum quoque crescere (sc. hominem) ultra jam prohibet. Quinta omne virium complet augmentum, sed à sexta usque ad septimam septimanam fit quidem diminutio, sed occulta. Ideò nonnullarum rerum publicarum is mos est, ut post sextam ad militiam nemo cogatur: in plurimis detur remissio justa post septimam.
units.tr: V. The total of the whole period is set forth with a certain holy sublimity of style, since the angel counts it not by years but by weeks [Hebrew] in the Septuagint [Greek]. The Vulgate has: "Seventy weeks are shortened." Commonly, among the Hebrews, week [Hebrew] denotes a span of seven days that continually returns in a circle, and to distinguish it from other kinds of weeks it is called a week of days [Hebrew]. Thus Daniel testifies that he was in mourning and fasting for three weeks of days [Hebrew] (Dan. x. 2, 3). Sometimes, however, in sacred usage it denotes a span of seven years, with a single day taken for each year, as happens often (Ezech. iv. 6; Apoc. xii. 6, etc.). Some draw here also that saying of Laban to Jacob: [Hebrew] "Fulfil this week", that is, this seven-year period, "and we will give you that one also" [Hebrew], "for the service in which you will serve with me yet seven other years" (Gen. xxix. 27). Here it is perhaps better to refer [Hebrew] to Leah, and to understand the week as the one appointed for her wedding; compare Gen. z. 10, Judg. xiv. 14, Tob. xi. 20. Others refer here that passage of Jeremiah, chapter v. 24, where God, rebuking the Jews for their great ingratitude, says that they do not call to mind that he gave them the early and late rain in its season, and that he kept for them the appointed weeks of the harvest [Hebrew]. But beyond all doubt is the passage Lev. xxv. 8: "And you shall number for yourself [Hebrew] seven sabbaths of years, seven years, seven times, and there will be for you [Hebrew] the days of the sabbaths of years, forty-nine years." A similar example of usage is brought forward by Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights iii. 10, from Marcus Varro, who somewhere testifies that he had now also entered his twelfth hebdomad of years, adding jokingly that up to that day he had written seventy hebdomads of books. Macrobius speaks similarly, Commentary on Scipio's Dream, Book v. chapter 6: "And when the fourth hebdomad of years is completed, it now forbids (man) to grow any further in breadth." The fifth completes all the increase of strength, but from the sixth to the seventh hebdomad there is indeed a decline, but a hidden one. Hence it is the custom of some commonwealths that after the sixth no one is compelled to military service; in most, a fair release is given after the seventh.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Praeter has duas septimanarum species, alias haud recenset Sacra Pagina. Unde septimanae decenniorum, quarum quaelibet sepries decem seu septuaginta annos contineret, & quas finxit, Origenes Homil. xxix. in Matth. aut etiam Jubilaeorum, imo saeculorum, ad quas desperatae causae indicio confugiunt quandoque Judaei, sicuti absque ullâ Scripturae authoritate excogitantur, ita eadem facilitate rejiciuntur, quâ prose-runtur. Remanet ergò ut vel hebdomadas dierum, vel annorum, intelligamus. Priores illae locum heic non reperiunt, quia scilicet spatium nimis breve continent, quam ut tot tantique eventus praedicti eo perfici possent. Praeterquam quod Daniel sequenti Capite tres dierum hebdomadas memorans, haud obscure illas ab hisce distinctas esse subinnuere voluerit. Subinde patet annorum hebdomadas esse intelligendas, consentientibus etiam in hoc Judaeorum plerisque Doctoribus.
units.tr: Besides these two kinds of weeks, Sacred Scripture recounts no others. Hence the weeks of decades, each of which would contain seven times ten, or seventy years, which Origen invented (Homily 29 on Matthew), or even weeks of jubilees, indeed of centuries, to which the Jews sometimes flee as a sign of a hopeless cause, are rejected with the same ease with which they are put forward, since they are devised without any authority of Scripture. It remains, therefore, that we understand either weeks of days or of years. The former find no place here, because they would contain too short a span for so many and such great events foretold to be accomplished in it. Moreover, Daniel, in the following chapter, mentioning three weeks of days, clearly meant to hint that those are distinct from these. Thereafter it is plain that weeks of years are to be understood, most of the Jewish teachers also agreeing in this.

units.la: VII. Quantum ad numerum porrò totalem septimanarum, declarat Angelus, eas à Deo decilas esse septuaginta, quæ communiter conficere creduntur annos 490. Hos verò quidam Lunares cum Julio Africano Sec. iii. Chronologo, ac Ven. Beda, plures Solares esse statuerunt. Et recte: notandum enim, quod quidem anni Lunares Veteribus Hebræis in usu fuerint, sic tamen ut iidem eos commoda intercalatione ad Solis motum revocaverint, uti ob festivitates anniversarias, annosque Sabbaticos, prorsus necessarium erat. Cucurrissent enim alias menses per omnes anni tempestates; nec Nisan אביב mensis spicarum semper esset Exod. xiii. 4. nec etiam postero die Paschatos, siquidem illud semper 14. vel 15. Nisan celebrari deberet, manipulus frugum maturescentium, aut festo Pentecostes primitiæ messis absolutæ offerri poterant, si non iidem menses intercalatione facta ad eandem anni tempestatem continuo rediissent. Eadem est ratio annorum Sabbaticorum; nam quovis septimo ineunte messis haud absoluta, aut etiam exeunte opportunum seminandi tempus pro anno octavo mox adesse poterat. Unde apparet, Judæos in digerendis annis suis ab uno Sabbatico in alium, & ab uno Jubileo in alium, non supputasse Lunares, sed necessario Solares annos; ac consequenter, cum hic Angelus numeret septuaginta annorum Sabbata, seu decem Jubileos, planum est utique quod non Lunares, sed Solares intelligat.
units.tr: VII. As to the total number of weeks, the angel declares that they have been decreed by God to be seventy, which are commonly believed to make 490 years. Some, however, with Julius Africanus, the third-century chronologer, and the Venerable Bede, have held that these are rather solar years. And rightly so: for it should be noted that although lunar years were in use among the ancient Hebrews, they nevertheless brought them back to the motion of the sun by a convenient intercalation, as was absolutely necessary for the annual festivals and the sabbatical years. For otherwise the months would have run through all the seasons of the year; nor would the month Nisan, the month of ears of grain [Hebrew] (Exod. xiii. 4), always be the month of ears; nor could a sheaf of ripening grain be presented on the day after the Passover, since that ought always to be celebrated on the 14th or 15th of Nisan, nor could the first-fruits of the harvest be offered at the feast of Pentecost, unless the same months, by intercalation, had continually returned to the same season of the year. The reasoning is the same for the sabbatical years; for in any seventh year the harvest would not be finished at its beginning, or at its end the opportune time for sowing for the eighth year could be at hand. Hence it appears that the Jews, in arranging their years from one sabbatical to another, and from one jubilee to another, did not reckon lunar years but necessarily solar years; and consequently, since here the angel counts seventy sabbaths of years, or ten jubilees, it is plain that he means solar, not lunar, years.

units.la: VIII. Ulteriori disquisitione indiget determinatio numeri annorum exsurgentium ex lxx. Hebdomadibus hisce. Certissimum est, si lxx. septimanæ invicem sibi immediatè subsequentes computentur, eas conficere annos 490. Verum si in ordine ad Judæorum computum eas numerari velit Angelus, ista annorum 490. determinatio extra omnem dubitationis aleam posita non erit. Numerabant enim Judæi juxta sententiam quorundam annos Sabbaticos, donec perventum esset ad septies septenum, id est quadragesimum nonum. Sequentem annum quinquagesimum faciunt Jubileum. Hunc verò in numero septenorum non fuisse, sed supputationem eorum rursus initium à quinquagesimo primo habuisse contendunt. Sic computasse Judæos autor est Maimonides. Cap. x. de Schemitta & Jubileo, cujus verba latinitate donata hunc in modum exhibet Vorstius
units.tr: VIII. The determination of the number of years arising from these seventy weeks requires further investigation. It is most certain that if the seventy weeks are counted as immediately following one another, they make 490 years. But if the angel wishes them to be counted in relation to the Jewish reckoning, the determination of these 490 years will not be placed beyond all risk of doubt. For the Jews, according to the opinion of some, used to count the sabbatical years until they reached seven times seven, that is the forty-ninth. The following fiftieth year they make the jubilee. But they contend that this was not among the sevens, but that the counting of the sevens began again from the fifty-first. That the Jews reckoned in this way is vouched for by Maimonides, chapter x. On the Sabbatical Year and the Jubilee, whose words, rendered into Latin, Vorstius presents in this way:

units.la: 𝔄 ... in Observat. ad Chronol. R. David Ganz. pag. 211. Annus Ju-bileus non resultat ex calculo annorum septimana, sed 49. annus Sabbaticus, & annus 50. Jubileus; 50. autem & posterior initium fit sex annorum septimana, atque sic deinceps in quolibet Jubileo. Huc etiam facere videtur Judæorum Chronologia in Seder Olam Rabba, ubi autor pro Jubileis xvii. putat annos Dcccl. cum anni decies septies xlix. facerent tantum annos Dcccxxxiii. Vide hoc notantem Cloppenburgium in Schola Sacrif. Cap. ii. §. xxviii. Nec absque ulla specie hoc ponitur. Etenim quod Jubileus non 49. sed 50. fuerit annus, præterquam quod aperte Moses annum 50. post numeratos annos 49. sanctificandum præscribat, satis colligi posse videtur exinde, quod expresse Deus in Jubileis tellurem coli prohibeat Levit. xxv. 11. 12. Quæ sanctio supervacanea videri posset, siquidem Jubileus in annum 49. incideret, quippe qui per se Sabbaticus, utpote septies septenus erat. Porro cum Jubileus annum septies Sabbaticum immediatè ex lege sequi, & tamen 50. anni ab uno ad alterum Jubileum, exclusò termino præcedentis, esse deberent, sequitur inde, quod Jubileus septies septenum immediatè semper sequi non possit, sed continuò ab illo divagari debeat, si nempe Jubileus primus esset in ordine septenorum. Unde concludere licet, illum 50. in ordine septenorum non fuisse, sed annos Sabbaticos à quinquagesimo primo demum numeratos esse. Quæ si vera sint, lxx. septimanæ, quatenus ita in orbem rediêre Judæis cum intercurrentibus Jubileis, jam non 490. sed 500. annos conficiunt; siquidem Angelus eam Judæorum computationem respiciat, atque illa computatio post captivitatem Babylonicam in usu fuerit, uti asserit idem Maimonides, Jubileos tum quidem non celebratos, attamen numeratos fuisse propter anni cujusvis septimi remissiones, quæ ex Lege fiebant. Non est profectò sententia hæc tanti ponderis, ut ob eam communem illam de numero annorum 490. deseramus. Utique probari nequit, singulos Jubileos comprehendisse annos 50. exclusò termino præcedentis. Quod gratis quidem in hac sententiâ supponitur. Dicitur quidem annus Jobel quinquagesimus, sed nil impedit quominus intelligatur cum inclusione termini præcedentis; sic ut primus Jubileus fuerit simul primus annus, non solum in ordine ad Sabbatibaticos, sed & ad Jubileum sequentem, ac proinde intervallum, quod intercedit ab uno Jubileo inclusive ad alterum fuerit tantum annorum 49. Et hoc pacto satis quidem sanctionum Divinarum de Jubileo quinquagesimo, & sequente continuo septies septenum, harmoniæ consulitur.
units.tr: "The jubilee year does not result from the calculation of the years of a week, but the forty-ninth year is a sabbatical year, and the fiftieth year a jubilee; and the fiftieth also becomes the beginning of a six-year week of years, and so on in every jubilee." (Vorstius, in Observations on the Chronology of R. David Ganz, p. 211). This also seems to favour the Jewish chronology in the Seder Olam Rabba, where the author, for seventeen jubilees, reckons 850 years, whereas the years of ten times forty-nine would make only 833. See Cloppenburg noting this in Schola Sacrificiorum, ch. ii. §28. Nor is this put forward without some show. For that the jubilee was not the forty-ninth but the fiftieth year, besides the fact that Moses clearly prescribes the fiftieth year to be sanctified after forty-nine years have been counted, seems sufficiently to be gathered from this, that God expressly forbids the land to be tilled in the jubilee (Lev. xxv. 11, 12). Which enactment might seem superfluous if the jubilee fell in the forty-ninth year, since that year is in itself sabbatical, being seven times seven. Further, since by law the jubilee must immediately follow the seventh sabbatical year, and yet the fifty years from one jubilee to the next, excluding the terminus of the preceding, ought to be the interval, it follows that the jubilee cannot always immediately follow seven times seven, but must continually stray from it, if indeed the first jubilee were in the order of sevens. Whence it may be concluded that that fiftieth year was not in the order of sevens, but that the sabbatical years were counted only from the fifty-first. If these things are true, the seventy weeks, insofar as they thus returned in a circle for the Jews with the intervening jubilees, now make not 490 but 500 years; provided the angel regards that Jewish reckoning, and provided that reckoning was in use after the Babylonian captivity, as the same Maimonides asserts, though the jubilees were then not celebrated, yet were counted on account of the remissions of every seventh year, which were made by the Law. This opinion is certainly not of such weight that on its account we should abandon the common view about the number of 490 years. Indeed it cannot be proved that the single jubilees comprised fifty years excluding the terminus of the preceding; this is assumed gratis in this opinion. The year is indeed called the fiftieth year of jubilee, but nothing prevents it being understood with the preceding terminus included; so that the first jubilee was at the same time the first year, not only in relation to the sabbaticals but also to the following jubilee, and consequently the interval from one jubilee, inclusive, to the next was only forty-nine years. And in this way harmony is secured with the divine enactments concerning the fiftieth jubilee and the following one, which continually falls in seven times seven.

units.la: I X. Interim quod Angelus hanc annorum summam LXX. hebdomadibus involverit, haud absque ratione factum putamus. Indicavit forte brevitatem temporis hujus, quod comparatè ad seculorum antelapsorum multitudinem, ac bonorum in ejus fine expectandorum magnitudinem, brevissimum ac quasi dierum vel septimanarum aliquot spatium haberi poterat. Sic utique Prophetæ præsertim post captivitatem Babylonicam brevem Messiæ moram, ad confirmandam fidelium fidem, eorumque consolationem augendam, adscribere solent Hagg. II. 8. Mal. III. 1. Eodem modo Angelus, cujus principale consilium est promittere Messiam, & liberationem spiritualem; ab ipso adducendam, uti ante dictum est, fluxuris ævis brevitatis quandam speciem conciliare forte voluit. Quod si alicui nimis argutum videatur, audiat aliam hujus rei causam, quam adfert Lud. Cappellus ad Tab. Chron. x. Observat ille, numerum hunc esse compositum ex duobus, septenario nimirum & denario, in se multiplicatis, atque illos duos numeros cum in Scriptura tum in natura esse insignes, ac à Deo quasi sanctificatos atque consecratos: propterea igitur Angelus iis hoc uti, quia hoc sapientiæ Dei consentaneum videtur, ut ad res tam insignes numerum etiam delegerit maxime insignem, ex duobus sacris & ab ipso sanctificatis numeris compositum. Magis ad rem docet Calvinus, Angelum hic alludere ad LXX. annos Captivitatis, de quibus verf. 2. atque eorum respectu heic promittere eum, quod misericordia Dei judicium ejus sit superatura septiplo, & duratura septies septuaginta annos ad Christum usque. Verba ejus inter alia sunt; Alludit quidem Propheta noster ad septuaginta annos Jeremia: & miror hoc à nostris non fuisse expensum? quia nemo est, qui causam afferat, cur annos supputet Daniel per hebdomadas. Addere licet, quod consultò Deus per annos Sabbaticos fluxuram abhinc annorum seriem usque ad Christum deduxerit, quia Christus in eorum fine adducturus erat שנת רצון, annum beneplaciti Jehovæ, in quo sanguine fuso, etiam in die Cippurim expiationis veræ, plenam ac veram שמטה / hoc est, omnium debitorum nostrorum remissionem, servitutis sub Diabolo ac peccato abolitionem, ac cælestium habitaculorum restitutionem mereretur, ac tuba Euangelii per omnem orbem proclamaret; quo & spectant forte sequentia Angeli verba mox explicanda.
units.tr: IX. We think it was not without reason that the angel comprised this sum of years in seventy weeks. Perhaps he thereby indicated the brevity of this time, which, compared with the multitude of past ages and the greatness of the good things to be expected at its end, could be regarded as very short, a span of a few days or weeks. The prophets, especially after the Babylonian captivity, commonly speak in this way of the brief delay of the Messiah, to confirm the faith of the faithful and increase their comfort (Hag. 2:8; Mal. 3:1). In the same way the angel, whose chief purpose is to promise the Messiah and spiritual deliverance to be brought by him, as was said above, may have wished to give the coming ages some appearance of brevity. If this seems to anyone too subtle, let him hear another reason for it, which Lud. Cappellus gives in his note on the Chronicle tables (x). He observes that this number is composed of two numbers, namely seven and ten, multiplied together, and that both these numbers are notable both in Scripture and in nature, and as it were hallowed and consecrated by God. Therefore the angel uses them for this reason, because it seems consistent with the wisdom of God that for matters so notable he should also choose a most notable number, composed of two sacred numbers which he himself has hallowed. Calvin teaches more to the point that the angel here alludes to the seventy years of captivity, mentioned in verse 2, and that with respect to them he promises here that the mercy of God will surpass his judgment sevenfold, and that the period will last seven times seventy years until Christ. Among other things his words are: "Our prophet certainly alludes to the seventy years of Jeremiah, and I wonder that this was not noticed by our people, for there is no one who gives a reason why Daniel reckons the years by weeks." It may be added that God deliberately carried the series of years flowing from that point down to Christ by means of the Sabbatical years, because Christ at their end was to bring the שנת רצון, the year of the good pleasure of Jehovah, in which, by the shedding of his blood, even on the day of the true atonement, Kippurim [כפורים], he would merit a full and true שמטה, that is, the remission of all our debts, the abolition of servitude under the Devil and sin, and the restoration of our heavenly dwellings, and would proclaim the trumpet of the Gospel throughout the whole world. To this perhaps also refer the words of the angel which are to be explained presently.

units.la: X. De his porro septimanis pronunciat Angelus, quod sint נחתך. Est vox hæc una ἐξ ἀπαξ λεγομένων, nec alibi in sacris occurrit.
units.tr: X. Concerning these weeks the angel further declares that they are נחתך [nechtak, "cut off" or "determined"]. This word is one of the hapax legomena [ἐξ ἀπαξ λεγομένων], and occurs nowhere else in Scripture.

units.la: Apud Rabbinos tamen frequens est sensu secandi, præcidendi &c. apud quos etiam voces derivatæ sunt חתך & חתיכה frustum, scissio, sectio. Convenit significatione juxta Kimchi cum גזר excidit, præcidit & juxta alios etiam cum חרץ, sensu eodem. Proprie ergo radix חתך notat scindere, resecare, præcidere &c. Quem significatum etiam LXX. exprimere voluerunt per suum συντεμνειν: licet enim συντέμνειν proprie concidere notet, LXX. tamen Interpretibus ut & aliis sæpe sumitur pro præcidere, abscindere Esa. x. 22. 23. Habent etiam voces synonymæ גזר & חרץ eleganti metaphora significatum decernendi ac definiendi: unde & idem huic nostro חתך denegari nequit ob analogiam. Atque hoc posteriori sensu vocem communiter Interpretes verterunt, definita, determinata, decreta, statuta sunt septimanæ LXX. Ita & Belga, sijn bestemt, communibus quasi calculis ordinatæ. Metaphoricam hanc significationem ita tamen à quibusdam urgeri nollemus, ut excludatur prorsus propria vocis notio, unde metaphora desumta est. Putamus enim hæc non debere sejungi, sed conjungi; ut dicat Angelus, LXX. Septimanæ decreto Numinis immutabili præcisæ, resectæ, abscissæ sunt. Utique si præcisæ sint, à quo ergo? nonne voluntate & decreto Dei qui tempora in manu sua habet; rursus si decretæ & definitæ sint, nonne vi vocis & metaphoræ ita decretæ, ut per hoc præcisæ sint ab omni tempore circumstanti? Vult ergo Angelus dicere, LXX. Septimanas immutabili voluntate divina statutas esse, ut certo fluant super populum Danielis, imo sic statutas esse, ut præcisæ ab omni alio tempore circumstanti nec plures nec pauciores fluxuræ sint. Nec quicquam obstat difficultas, quam movet Raynoldus, quasi si præcisè urgeremus vocis significationem, atque ita ut non solum definire & statuere, verum etiam præcisè statuere ac dedefinire significet, non essent anni 490. sed pauciores. Nam, inquit, decidere aut præcidere est aliquid ex ipsa summa detrahere. Id verum quidem est, sed ita applicandum necessario huic rei, ut dicimus, LXX. has septimanas decreto Dei esse præcisas & amputatas ex majori temporis summâ, quam quidem, si ita lubuisset, constituere potuisset Deus. Illud enim quod præciditur, amputatur modo ab omni re circumstanti, ac per id terminos suos & fines suos proprios accipit. Quo sensu verbum abbreviare forte sumsit Latinus Interpres, ut idem sit ac aliquid amputare de toto, quod eatenus abbreviatur, quatenus suos terminos accipit, ac unum continuum cum toto esse desinit. Ita Corn. à Lapide, qui ut versionem hanc suam Vulgatam in commodum sensum pertrahat, hedomadas abbreviatas dici putat, quòd pauca septimana definitæ sunt usque ad Christum, cum Deus longè plures potuisset statuere. Notari tandem meretur constructio irregularis, juxta quam verbum נחחך in singulari jungitur nomini plurali. Qualis constructionis Hebræis & Græcis haud infrequentis exempla alia produxere Grammatici Vid. Glass. Lib. III. Tract. III. Can. LII. Hoc fieri creditur, quando aliquid non modo ad universos, sed & distributivè ad singulos referri debet; sic Gen. XLIX. 22. בנוח צערה עלי שור filia (sc. vitis id est rami ejus) procedit supra murum, id est, unaquaque earum procedit. Itaque hac constructione denotarur particularis decisio ac determinatio, non tantum universæ summæ LXX. hebdomadum, sed & singularum in ista summa partium, quin & annorum, ita ut ne quidem unus vel addi vel demi debeat. Alias constructio hæc fundatur in septimarum collectione in unum temporis spatium.
units.tr: Among the rabbis, however, it is frequently used in the sense of cutting, cutting off, etc., and from it are derived the words חתך and חתיכה [chathichah], a piece, a cutting, a section. According to Kimchi it agrees in meaning with גזר [gazar], to cut off, to sever, and according to others also with חרץ [charats], in the same sense. Properly, then, the root חתך signifies to cut, to cut away, to cut off, etc. The Seventy also wished to express this meaning by their συντεμνειν [suntemnein]; for although συντέμνειν properly means to cut in pieces, the Seventy translators, as others too, often use it for to cut off, to cut away (Isa. 10:22, 23). The synonymous words גזר and חרץ also have by an elegant metaphor the meaning of deciding and defining, so that by analogy the same sense cannot be denied to this word חתך. And it is in this latter sense that the Interpreters commonly translated the word: the weeks of the Seventy are defined, determined, decreed, fixed. So too the Dutch, sijn bestemt, arranged as it were by common reckonings. We would not wish this metaphorical meaning to be pressed by some so that the proper notion of the word, from which the metaphor is taken, is entirely excluded. For we think these should not be separated but joined, so that the angel says: the seventy weeks have been cut, cut off, severed by the immutable decree of the Deity. For if they are cut off, from what are they cut off? Surely by the will and decree of God, who holds times in his hand. Again, if they are decreed and defined, is it not by the force of the word and the metaphor that they are so decreed that by this they are cut off from all surrounding time? The angel therefore means that the seventy weeks have been fixed by the immutable divine will, so that they flow certainly over the people of Daniel; indeed they are so fixed that, cut off from all other surrounding time, they are to flow neither more nor fewer. Nor does the difficulty which Raynold raises stand in the way, as if if we pressed the signification of the word precisely, so that it meant not only to define and to fix but also precisely to fix and to undefine, the years would not be 490 but fewer. For, he says, to cut off or to sever is to take something away from the total sum. This is indeed true, but it must be applied to this matter in the way that we say that the Seventy weeks have been severed and cut off by God's decree from a greater sum of time, which indeed God could have appointed had he so wished. For what is cut off is simply separated from everything around it, and so receives its own proper terms and limits. In this sense the Latin translator perhaps took the verb to abbreviate, so that it means the same as to cut something off from a whole, which is thereby shortened in so far as it receives its own limits and ceases to be one continuous thing with the whole. So Cornelius à Lapide, who, to bend his Vulgate version to a convenient sense, thinks the weeks are said to be abbreviated, because only a few weeks have been defined until Christ, whereas God could have appointed far more. Finally, the irregular construction deserves to be noted, by which the verb נחתך is joined in the singular to a plural noun. Grammarians have brought forward other examples of this construction, not infrequent among Hebrews and Greeks (see Glassius, Book III, Tract III, Canon LII). This is believed to occur when something must be referred not only to all together but distributively to each single item; thus in Gen. 49:22, בנות צעדה עלי שור, the daughter (that is, its branches) walks upon the wall, that is, each of them walks. By this construction, therefore, a particular decision and determination is denoted, not only of the whole sum of the seventy weeks, but also of the individual parts of that sum, and even of the years, so that not even one of them may be added or taken away. Otherwise this construction is based on the gathering of the weeks into one span of time.

units.la: XI. Subjectum porro, ad quod hæc temporis mensura extrinsecus ordinata est, est Populus Judaicus, & Sancta Hierosolyma.
units.tr: XI. Next, the subject to which this measure of time is externally assigned is the Jewish people and the holy Jerusalem.

units.la: Ita porro habet sacer textus על עמך ועל־עיר קדשך super populum tuum & super civitatem sanctitatis tuam. Videtur Clar. L. Empereur urbem à sanctitate distinguere, quando hunc in modum super hæc verba commentatur; Septimanæ 70. à Deo justæ destinatæ & consilio æterno præcisæ, quibus populus tuus Judaicus ædificet, & deinde ut vera Ecclesia inhabitet civitatem Jerusalem, una cum sanctitate tua, id est Templo Sanctissimo. Verum absque ulla necessitate ellipsis conjunctionis sic in textum intruditur, multoque convenientius vox קדשך ut nomen rectum antecedenti עיר ut voci regenti subjungitur, sicuti aperte satis Angelus, bis repetita praepositione על, non tria, sed duo tantum orationis membra facit. Affixum porro ך, quod nomini recto adhaeret, ad regens referri debet, ut commodus inde sensus oriatur, unde vertenda verba sunt super urbem sanctitatis, non tua, sed tuam. Constructionis hujus alia exempla dant Grammatici. E plurimis haec duo habe. Quum invoco, exaudi me אלהי צדקי Deus justitiae meae, id est, mi Deus justitia, seu justissime Pf. iv. 1. Rursus Pf. lix. 11. juxta תו Keri, & 18. אלהי חסדי Deus benignitatis meae, id est, mi Deus benignitatis, seu benignissime. Est & alius Hebraismus, quando civitas sanctitatis ponitur pro civitate sancta. Sic enim Hebraeis familiare est Vir fortitudinis, violentiae &c. Deus benignitatis, justitia, pro viro forti, violento &c. Deo benigno, justo &c. Uti porro populus Judaicus, non obstante captivitate duta, Dei populus manserat verf. 15. 16. 19. ob foedus cum ipsis olim erectum, neutiquam a parte Dei, etiamsi severe castigantis, ruptum, ita etiam populus Danielis recte vocatur ab Angelo. Quod fieri credimus, eam ob causam, quia conterranei erant, ac ejusdem stemmatis cum Daniele Judaei; magis vero, quia eodem rege ac eadem lege uniti, gentem sanctam בגלה Dei, ac λαὸν περιούσιον ex omnibus aliis populis singulariter hactenus electum constituebant, ac ea propter ipse Daniel eorum causam apud Deum egerat conf. Exod. xxxii.7. Jerusalem perinde, uti civitas sancta saepius vocatur, etiam qualis erat post captivitatem Babylonicam Matth. iv.5. xxvii. 53. &c. ita revera sic dici heic meretur. Equidem segregata olim ad cultum Dei, ejus nunc publica sedes rursus futura erat, eligente eam Jehovah Zach. iii.2. ut mensam quotidie ibi instructam, ignem focumque suum iterum haberet, non obstante quorundam gloriosae praesentiae suae symbolorum forte defectu. Ad eam quoque pertinebat Daniel jure nativitatis forsan in ea, saltem jure religionis, ut Israelita, quorum omnium communis urbs Jerusalem, atque pro ea restauranda precibus calidis apud Deum intercesserat, unde & Angelus super civitatem sanctam tuam dicit. Quod affixum lxx. ex Editione Romana, ut & Clemens Alex. ac Tertullianus quoad posterius membrum non expresserunt.
units.tr: The sacred text reads: super populum tuum and super civitatem sanctitatis tuam [על עמך ועל־עיר קדשך], "upon your people and upon the city of your holiness." The illustrious L. Empereur seems to separate the city from holiness, when he comments on these words as follows: Seventy weeks, decreed by God and cut off by his eternal counsel, in which your Jewish people shall build, and afterwards, as the true Church, shall dwell in the city of Jerusalem together with your holiness, that is, the most holy Temple. But this inserts an ellipsis of the conjunction into the text with no necessity. It is much more fitting to join the word קדשך as a genitive to the preceding word עיר, which is the governing noun. The Angel makes this plain by repeating the preposition על twice, so that he makes not three members of the sentence but only two. The suffixed ך, which attaches to the genitive noun, must be referred back to the governing noun, so that a suitable sense arises. Hence the words should be rendered upon the city of holiness, with the suffix meaning your city, not your holiness. Grammarians give other examples of this construction, and two of the many may suffice. When I call, hear me [Ps. 4:1], אלהי צדקי, the God of my righteousness, that is, my God of righteousness, or most righteous. Again, Ps. 59:11 according to the Keri, and verse 18, אלהי חסדי, the God of my kindness, that is, my God of kindness, or most kind. There is also another Hebraism, where a city of holiness is put for a holy city. Thus it is familiar to the Hebrews to say a man of strength, of violence, and so on, and a God of kindness, of justice, meaning a strong man, a violent man, a kind God, a just God. Moreover, just as the Jewish people, though carried into captivity, remained the people of God (vv. 15, 16, 19) on account of the covenant once made with them, a covenant never broken on God's side, even though he chastised them severely, so too the Angel rightly calls them the people of Daniel. We believe this was so for the reason that the Jews were compatriots of Daniel and of the same stock. More importantly, united under the same king and the same law, they constituted the holy nation, the people of God's own possession (λαὸν περιούσιον), singled out from all other peoples until then, and for this reason Daniel himself had pleaded their cause before God (cf. Exod. 32:7). Jerusalem likewise, which is often called the holy city (Matth. 4:5; 27:53, etc.), deserves to be called so here, even as it was after the Babylonian captivity. Indeed, having once been set apart for the worship of God, it was to become again his public seat, Jehovah choosing it (Zech. 3:2), so that it would again have a table set daily, his fire and hearth, though some tokens of his glorious presence might perhaps be lacking. Daniel too belonged to it, perhaps by right of birth in it, or at least by right of religion, as an Israelite; for Jerusalem was the common city of all of them, and he had interceded before God with warm prayers for its restoration. That is why the Angel also says your holy city. The Septuagint from the Roman edition does not express this suffix, nor do Clement of Alexandria and Tertullian express the latter member.

units.la: XII. Quando jam super hunc populum, urbemque sanctam
units.tr: XII. When now over this people and the holy city

units.la: LXX. septimanæ præcisè decretæ dicuntur, supponitur Hiero-solymam jam solo æquatam ac cineribus obrutam mox restau-randam, unà cum Templo, ut sit civitas & quidem sancta, ad cultum Dei publicum segregata, in qua Sancto Israelis sacra facere ac victimas denuò epulari fas esset, atque a populo hoc rursus eam inhabitandam fore. Innuitur porrò, eatenus populum ac civitatem esse subjecta hujus temporis, quatenus rursus conjuncta ac in integrum restituta sint: ut adeo hæ hebdomadæ non possint videri lapsæ esse vel totaliter, vel quoad notabilem annorum partem, quando populus nondum est reductus, & urbs necdum cæpta ædificari; sed initium demum sumant à verbo liberationis, ac illud mox secuta reductione populi ad civitatem sanctam inhabitandam & reædificandam; quod factum non est intra unius anni breve spatium. Declarat tandem Angelus characterem termini septimanarum harum, ac mensuram durationis populi ac civitatis sanctæ sic circumscribit. LXX. nempe septimanas constituerat Deus, ut fluerent super eam; quibus finitis finem quoque suum sortiri debebat. Equidem determinare certum ac præcisum tempus super aliquid, quid aliud notare potest, quam tantum temporis ei dare & concedere, quo duret adhuc, & quo ad finem lapso, esse quoque desinat? Nec objici debet, non legi heic absolute LXX. septimanas esse decisas super populum & civitatem sanctam, sed expresso addito termino, usque ad claudendam prævaricationem &c. quam interpretationem Tremellii laudat & sequitur Pareus. Non enim sufficit ita posse forsan, sed & debere heic verti præfixum ⌉ Patebit mox significationem hujus præfixi finalem usitatissimam præferendam esse; nec Angelum dicere LXX. Septimanas decisas esse super urbem sanctam usque ad illa beneficia, sed ut illa adducantur per Messiam in fine earum. Ita verò mensuram durationis populi ac civitatis sanctæ heic reperimus, ut tamen non colligamus hinc cum Scaligero, Calvisio, aliisque, terminum septimanarum harum esse excidium populi & urbis finale & totale per Romanos. Sed id contendimus, quod Judæi hisce Dei verbis ab Angelo edoceantur, quamdiu peculiaris Dei populus jure vocari possent, atque Jerusalem eorum civitas pro sancta, id est, ad cultum Dei publicum segregata jure habenda esset, nimirum LXX. annorum hebdomadas: Harum itaque finis tum erit, quando Judæi se ipsos abdica- bunt regimine Dei, ac Regem suum ac rupem salutis suæ pro- terve rejicient, clamantes οὐκ ἔχομεν βασιλέα εἰ μὴ καίσαρα. Joh. xix. 15. quando Messias hic promissus sacrificio corpo- ris sui oblato cessare faciet sacrificium & munus, quæ hactenus sanctitatem Hierosolymæ dederant, ac intergerino illo cære- moniarum pariete per crucem in carne sua fracto inimicitiam in- ter Judæos ac gentiles abolebit pace facta; quando denique Messias princeps factus atque exaltatus Spiritum suum mittet ex alto, atque relicto Templo materiali, impositerum corda solum- modò fidelium in Templa sacrosancta sibi per eum consecrare, simul etiam sceptrum potentiæ suæ è Tsione protendere, ac Euan- gelium regni sui, quod est libertatis, annunciare incipiet. Aperte Angelus in hisce rebus finem septimanarum ponit in se- quentibus, uti videbimus. Et hæc cuncta ejus naturæ esse, ut præ- rogativam Judaicæ gentis, tanquam populi Dei peculiaris, ac Hierosolymæ, tanquam Civitatis Sanctæ, enervent, comproba- runt prodigia, quæ in urbe ista eodem tempore facta sunt. Lace- ratio veli, Sancto Sanctorum obtensi, circa mortem Christi, dictabat, terrestre Tabernaculum non amplius pro habiraculo suo sancto haberi velle Deum, expiationes annuas & cultus Levi- ticos, quamvis eos de facto adhuc aliquot annos toleraret, inu- tiles tamen, nec sibi acceptos fore, propter sanguinem Filii sui fusum, qui taurorum ac hircorum illum sistere debebat. Inter ostenta miserandæ ac ultimæ gentis hujus excisionis memo- rat Josephus etiam vocem die quodam Pentecostes sacro, à sa- cerdotibus, nocte interius Templi septum ad sacra celebranda ingressis, post motum strepitumque animad versum primò, au- ditam, quæ clamabat, Migremus hinc. de Bello Judaico. Lib. vii. Cap. 12. Hieronymus ad tempus passionis Domini hoc refert, uti & Eusebius facere videtur in Chronico ad annum Domini xxxiii. quod perstringens Casaubonus confidenter hoc prodigium anno ante captam everlamque urbem sexto, Christi 65. adscribit, Excercit xvi. §. xcviii. ad Annales Ecclef. Baronii. Cum annum, quo id factum est, non noret Josephus, inquit Lud. Cappellus in hist. Jud. Comp. p. 135. suspicari quis non immerito possit, corrigisse id die illo Pentecostes, quo Spiritus Sanctus in Apostolos à Christo missus est. Tum enim proprie videtur HaHaschecinah Judaeos & Templum deseruisse, ut ad Christi Discipulos transmigraret. Atque hæc vox apertum est rejectionis Judæorum & totius legalis cultus abolitionis Testimonium. Quam Cappelli observationem non negligendam dicit Cloppenburgius, licet addat suam Disput. Select. XI. §. XXXII. Prædictio verò talis de abolendis ceremoniis atque discutiendis umbris præsentiam corporis ipsius & adventum Messiæ exspectatum includit. Unde gravis ea esse nequit Israeli vero, sed defectori quidem & stupido, terrena magis quam cælestia, corticem quam nucleum ambienti. Etenim verus Israel cerimonias legales ac urbem terrestrem unicè amat propter Messiam, per eas præfiguratum, ac hac stante manifestandum, quo exhibito, non amplius τῳ νῦν sed τῳ ἄνω Ιερουσαλὴμ quærit ac desiderat.
units.tr: The seventy weeks are said to be precisely decreed. This presupposes that Jerusalem, already levelled with the ground and buried in ashes, is soon to be restored together with the Temple, so that it may again be a city indeed holy, set apart for the public worship of God, in which it would be lawful to perform sacred rites for the Holy One of Israel and to feast again on the sacrifices, and in which the people would again dwell. It is further implied that the people and the city are subject to this period only so far as they are reunited and restored to their former state. Thus these weeks cannot be thought to have lapsed either wholly or for any considerable part of the years, when the people has not yet been brought back and the city has not yet been begun to be built. Rather, they take their start from the word of liberation, and that is followed soon by the return of the people to inhabit and rebuild the holy city, which did not happen within the short space of a single year. Finally, the Angel declares the character of the limit of these weeks, and thus marks off the measure of the duration of the people and the holy city. God, he says, has determined seventy weeks to run over it; when these are finished, it too must come to its end. For what else can it mean to determine a certain and precise time over anything, than to give and grant it only so much time that it may last, and that when that time has run out it may also cease to be? Nor should it be objected that the text does not read here that the seventy weeks are cut off absolutely over the people and the holy city, but with a limit expressly added: until the transgression is closed up, etc. This is the rendering that Tremellius praises and follows, and Pareus too. It is not enough that the prefixed ⌉ could perhaps be translated so; it must be so translated here. It will soon be clear that the final meaning of this prefix is to be preferred, as the most common usage. The Angel does not say that the seventy weeks are cut off over the holy city until those benefits, but so that those benefits are brought in by the Messiah at their end. Yet we do not infer from this measure of the duration of the people and the holy city, as Scaliger, Calvisius and others do, that the limit of these weeks is the final and total destruction of the people and the city by the Romans. We contend rather that by these words of God the Jews are taught by the Angle how long the people of God could rightly be called peculiar, and how long Jerusalem as their city was rightly to be regarded as holy, that is, set apart for the public worship of God. This is, namely, seventy weeks of years. Its end, therefore, will come when the Jews renounce the government of God themselves, and stubbornly reject their King and the rock of their salvation, crying out, We have no king but Caesar [οὐκ ἔχομεν βασιλέα εἰ μὴ καίσαρα] (Joh. 19:15); when this promised Messiah, by the offering of his body in sacrifice, shall cause sacrifice and oblation to cease, which until then had given holiness to Jerusalem; when, breaking down in his flesh through the cross that dividing wall of ceremonies, he abolishes the enmity between Jews and Gentiles and makes peace; and finally, when the Messiah, made prince and exalted, sends his Spirit from on high, and, leaving the material Temple, begins to consecrate for himself, through himself, the hearts of the faithful alone as holy temples, and at the same time to stretch out the sceptre of his power from Zion and to proclaim the gospel of his kingdom, which is the gospel of liberty. The Angel clearly places the end of the seven weeks in these events, as we shall see below. That all these things are of such a nature as to undermine the privilege of the Jewish nation as the peculiar people of God, and of Jerusalem as the holy city, is confirmed by the portents that occurred in that city at the same time. The rending of the veil, which hung before the Holy of Holies, around the death of Christ, signified that God no longer wished the earthly tabernacle to be regarded as his holy dwelling place; that the annual expiations and Levitical worship, although for some years he still in fact tolerated them, would be useless and unacceptable to him because of the blood of his Son that had been shed, which was to take the place of the blood of bulls and goats. Among the omens of the pitiable and final destruction of this nation, Josephus also records a voice heard on a certain day of the sacred feast of Pentecost. The priests, having entered by night into the inner court of the Temple to celebrate the sacred rites, first noticed a movement and a noise, and then heard a voice crying, Let us depart from here [Migremus hinc] (de Bello Judaico, book 7, chapter 12). Jerome refers this to the time of the Lord's passion, as Eusebius also seems to do in the Chronicle at the year of the Lord 33. Casaubon, criticising this, confidently assigns this portent to the year 65 of Christ, one year before the capture and overthrow of the city (Exercitation 16, §98, on Baronius's Annals of the Church). Since Josephus did not know the year in which this happened, says Ludwig Cappel in his History of the Jews, p. 135, one may not unreasonably suspect that he got the day of Pentecost wrong, the day on which the Holy Spirit was sent by Christ upon the Apostles. For then it seems that the Shechinah properly left the Jews and the Temple, so as to pass over to the disciples of Christ. And this voice is a clear testimony to the rejection of the Jews and the abolition of the whole legal worship. Cloppenburg says that this observation of Cappel's is not to be neglected, although he adds his own remark (Disputationes selectae XI, §32). Such a prediction about the abolition of the ceremonies and the removal of the shadows includes the presence of Christ's own body and the expected coming of the Messiah. Therefore it cannot be grave for a true Israelite, but only for an apostate and dull person, one who cares more for earthly things than heavenly, who embraces the husk rather than the kernel. For the true Israel loves the legal ceremonies and the earthly city solely on account of the Messiah, who was prefigured through them and was to be made manifest while that city stood; when he was revealed, the true Israel no longer seeks and desires the present Jerusalem [τῳ νῦν] but the Jerusalem above [τῳ ἄνω Ιερουσαλὴμ].

units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Videtur quidem Christus sanctitatem adhuc tribuere Hierosolymæ, quando ab Romano excercitu cincta, jam delenda erat: Quum ergo videritis τὸ βδέλυγμα τῆς ἐρημώσεως ἑστὼς ἐν τόπῳ ἁγίῳ abominationem desolationis stantem in loco sancto Matth. XXIV. 15. Verum animadvertendum est, sanctitatem urbi competiisse eò tempore, quo Christus hæc prænunciabat, & à præsenti prærogativa illum urbem circumscribere. Nec repugno, quod Christus ita urbem appellare potuerit, etiam cum respectu ad id tempus, quo à milite Romano obsessa erat; siquidem hodie etiam Palæstinam terram sanctam nominare possumus, & nominamus vulgò, non quod talis hactenus sit, sed olim fuerit. Et cum de facto urbem Templum ac cultum Leviticum tolerarit Deus, licet de jure abrogatum, usque ad πανωλεθρίαν reipublicæ Judaicæ, ut honestè sepeliriretur vetus Synagoga, mansit eo sensu quadantenus civitas sancta & magni Regis, quamdiu mansit.
units.tr: Christ seems still to ascribe holiness to Jerusalem, when it was already surrounded by the Roman army and about to be destroyed: When therefore you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place (Matth. XXIV. 15) [τὸ βδέλυγμα τῆς ἐρημώσεως ἑστὼς ἐν τόπῳ ἁγίῳ]. But it must be noted that the holiness belonged to the city at the time when Christ was foretelling these things, and he describes the city by its present privilege. Nor do I object that Christ could so call the city even with reference to the time when it was besieged by the Roman soldier, since today too we can call Palestine the holy land, and we commonly do so, not because it is such now, but because it once was. And since God, though the law was abrogated, tolerated the Temple and the Levitical worship in fact until the utter destruction [πανωλεθρίαν] of the Jewish state, so that the old Synagogue might be honourably buried, the city remained in a certain sense holy and the city of the great King for as long as it remained.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Totum hoc intervallum dederat Deus Judæis, ut consilium suum de liberatione peccatoris per sanguinem Filii sui exequeretur. Ideo pergit Angelus, לכלא הפשע ולחתם חטאות ולכפר עון ולהביא צדק עלמים ולחתם חזון ונביא ולמשח קדש קדשים Ad claudendum defectionem, & ad obsignandum peccata, & ad expiandum iniquitatem, & ad adducendum justitiam seculorum; & ad obsignandum visionem & Prophetam, & ad ungendum Sanctum Sanctorum. Totidem hæc sunt beneficia, olim adducenda, quorum intuitu has LXX. sep-aimaaimanas populo Judaico Deus concesserat. In his recensendis eum servat ordinem Angelus, ut primo quæ mala auferenda, deinde quæ bona adferenda essent declaret.
units.tr: God had granted the Jews this whole interval so that his counsel concerning the deliverance of the sinner through the blood of his Son might be carried out. Therefore the Angel goes on: To finish the transgression, and to seal up sins, and to make atonement for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal up vision and prophet, and to anoint the Most Holy [לכלא הפשע ולחתם חטאות ולכפר עון ולהביא צדק עלמים ולחתם חזון ונביא ולמשח קדש קדשים]. These are as many benefits, to be brought in time, for the sake of which God had granted the Jewish people these seventy weeks. In enumerating them the Angel keeps this order, so that he first declares which evils are to be removed and then which goods are to be brought.

units.la: X V. Ante omnia inquirendum est in significationem præfixi ⳮ. Supra attigimus Tremellium, eumque secutum Pareum, id vertere per usque ad, ut sic notetur terminus ad quem septimanarum duratio extensa esset. Eodem sensu legitur apud Theodoretum, ἕως δ᾽ ἂν παλαιωθῇναι τὸ πρόσκτωμα; similiter & apud Tertullianum, Quoad usque inveteretur delictum. Non caret forte exemplo usus præfixi talis cum infinitivo constructi. Conferri possunt Levit. xxiv. 12. 2 Chron. xxxvi. 21, Jef. vii. 15. &c. Longe frequentius tamen præfixum hoc usurpatur ad denotandam causam finalem, cujus gratia aliquid fit. Exempla adducere in re nota supervacaneum est. Atque ita rem intellexerunt vulgò Interpretes, quorum alii gerundium in dum, allii conjunctionem ut adhibuerunt. Graci δ᾽ συντελεσθῆναι, ὡς σφεγχάσι &c. Hoc posterius præferendum judicamus, siquidem sic Angeli responsio belle convenit cum petitione Danielis. Hic petierat urbis ac populi restitutionem propter Dominum; Ille declarat futuram eandem propter Dominum, opusque gratiæ ab ipso consummandum. Scilicet exigebat Divini consilii ratio, ut promissus Messias intra limites terræ Canaanis appareret; unde terra Immanuelis dicitur Jef. viii. 1. Semen illud Abrahamo promissum ibi oriundum erat; quod credidit ille, quando exiens è terrâ suâ in peregrinis illis oris tentoria fixit Heb. xi. 1. 9. Postulabat itidem prorsus divina veritas, ut Dominator Israelis prodiret ex Bethlehem, tanquam civitate tribus Judæ, atque reipublicæ Judaicæ membro Mich. v. 1. & ut in Tsion germinaret cornu Davidis, quod sceptrum potentiæ suæ, verbum Evangelii inde potenderet, ac ibi latissimi imperii sui fundamenta jaceret Pf. cx. 2. cxxxii. 17. Jef. ii. 3. Mich. iv. 2. Necessum ergo erat ut Judæi reducerentur in terram hanc patriam, & Tsion ac Templum reædificarentur, & starent in adventu Messiæ, qui ibi nasci, versari, salutem operari, ac regnum auspicari debebat. Hinc est quod pronunciat Angelus septimanas lxx. datas esse populo reducto & urbi sanctæ instauratæ, ut, nimirum per Messiam principem, interea elaudatur defectio. Neque tantum hoc in loco, sed & alibi Deus potum notum fecit Judæis, se captivitatem illorum in Babel non re-laxasse intuitu dignitatis aut meriti in ipsis, sed propter Christum & futuram ab ipso redemtionem, quatenus etiam apud ipsos reductos in terram peragi deberet. Præter Ief. x. 2. aliaque, locus in hanc rem est notabilis Zach. ix. 11. Etiam Tu, (ô Filia Sion) in sanguine fœderis tui emisi vinctos tuos è fovea, in qua non est aqua. Horum verborum amplam exegesin hic addere chartæ angustia prohibet.
units.tr: XV. Before all else we must inquire into the meaning of the prefixed ad (ʿad). Above we touched on Tremellius, and Pareus following him, who render it until, so that the terminus to which the duration of the weeks was extended is marked. In the same sense it is read in Theodoret: until the sin grows old [ἕως δ᾽ ἂν παλαιωθῇναι τὸ πρόσκτωμα]; similarly in Tertullian: until the offence grows old. Perhaps such a use of the prefix with the infinitive is not without precedent. Compare Levit. xxiv. 12; 2 Chron. xxxvi. 21; Jef. vii. 15, etc. Far more often, however, this prefix is used to denote the final cause, for the sake of which something is done. It is superfluous to adduce examples in a well-known matter. And so the common interpreters understood the matter, some using the gerund in -dum, others the conjunction that. The Greek [συντελεσθῆναι] ... We judge the latter to be preferable, since the Angel's answer then agrees well with Daniel's petition. Daniel had asked for the restoration of the city and people for the Lord's sake; the Angel declares that it will be so, again for the Lord's sake, and for the work of grace to be accomplished by him. Clearly the plan of the divine counsel required that the promised Messiah should appear within the bounds of the land of Canaan; hence the land is called the land of Immanuel (Jef. viii. 1). The seed promised to Abraham was to arise there; he believed this when, leaving his own land, he pitched his tents in those foreign regions (Heb. xi. 1, 9). Likewise divine truth absolutely demanded that the Ruler of Israel should come forth from Bethlehem, a city of the tribe of Judah and a member of the Jewish state (Mich. v. 1); and that the horn of David should sprout in Zion, so that from there it might stretch out the sceptre of his power, the word of the Gospel, and there lay the foundations of his most wide-reaching empire (Ps. cx. 2; cxxxii. 17; Jef. ii. 3; Mich. iv. 2). It was therefore necessary that the Jews be brought back into this native land, and that Zion and the Temple be rebuilt, and that they stand at the coming of the Messiah, who was to be born there, live there, work salvation there, and inaugurate his kingdom. Hence the Angel declares that the seventy weeks are given to the people restored and to the city renewed, so that, namely, through the Messiah the prince, in the meantime the transgression may be finished. God made this known to the Jews not only in this place but also elsewhere: he had not relaxed their captivity in Babylon out of regard for any dignity or merit in them, but on account of Christ and the redemption to be made by him, which was also to be carried out among them after their return to the land. Besides Jef. x. 2 and others, a notable passage on this point is Zach. ix. 11: As for you also, O daughter of Zion, by the blood of your covenant I have sent forth your prisoners out of the pit in which there is no water. The narrowness of this page forbids me to add here a full exposition of these words.

units.la: XVI. Sed progredimur ad ipsa beneficia.
units.tr: XVI. But we proceed to the benefits themselves.

units.la: Ut eò melius sensum verborum sequentium assequamur, non inutile erit, priusquam sententiam nostram promamus, audire quid alii dixerint. Quod ut commodè fiat, non ad singula versus enunciata carptim aliorum exegeses annotare, sed ad universa eas complexim exhibere animus est. Audiamus ergo primò Judæos. Jachiades, postquam LXX. שמיטות à tempore vastationis ædis primæ, usque ad vastationem ædis secundæ, numerandas esse inculcasset, atque פשע peccatum במחשבה cogitatione commissum, juxta Ps. XXXVI. 2. חטאה peccatum במעשה opere externo patratum, juxta Prov. I. 10. עון peccatum ברבור sermone externo prolatum esse, notasset; addit, ex versione Clar. L'Empereur, (quam solam exhibebo, ne Lectori utriusque textus citatione gravis fiam,) in captivitate Babylonica iniquitates & peccata consumpta non fuisse. Nam ecce, inquit, postea in æde secunda denuò redierunt ad peccandum, quemadmodum prius. Sed in exilio hoc secundo consumentur atque finientur omnes iniquitates: quia tam grave exilium expiabit iniquitatem; nec peccabit amplius Israelitica domus. Quocirca sub finem illius regnum quintum adveniet Israelitis, & adducetur Justitia, id est tabula ædis æterna in Sanctuarium, quæ defuerunt in æde secunda, & obsignabitur atque sigillabitur visio & Propheta, quia effunder Deus Spiritum suum super omnem carnem, & filii somnia somniabunt, ætatis quamvis immaturæ, cum in æde secunda defecerit Prophetia. Et ad ungendum Sanctitatem Sanctitatum oleo unctionis, quum defecerit hoc oleum in æde secunda. Consentit fere Menasseh Ben Israël. de Term. Vita Lib. III. Sect. VI. §. VI. Hebdomades se tuaginta &c. Hic illi denuntiatur præsens libertas, & futura aliquando nova ac dura populi captivitas, per quam ab omni peccatorum reatu Israël mundaretur. Et paucis inter-
units.tr: So that we may better grasp the sense of the words that follow, it will not be unhelpful, before we set out our own view, to hear what others have said. To do this conveniently, I intend not to note the separate expositions of others verse by verse, but to set out their views together as a whole. Let us hear the Jews first. Jachiades, after insisting that the seventy sabbatical years [שמיטות] are to be counted from the destruction of the first temple to the destruction of the second, and after noting that transgression [פשע] is sin committed in thought [במחשבה], according to Ps. 36:2; that offence [חטאה] is sin committed in outward act [במעשה], according to Prov. 1:10; and that iniquity [עון] is sin uttered in outward speech [בדבור], adds, from the translation of Clar. L'Empereur, (which alone I shall give, so as not to burden the reader with citing both texts), that iniquities and sins were not brought to an end during the Babylonian captivity. "For behold," he says, "afterwards in the second temple they returned again to sinning, just as before. But in this second exile all iniquities will be consumed and brought to an end, because so grievous an exile will atone for iniquity, and the house of Israel will sin no more. Therefore at the end of that time the fifth kingdom will come to Israel, and Righteousness will be brought in, that is, the eternal tablet in the Sanctuary, which was lacking in the second temple. The vision and the prophet will be sealed and signed, because God will pour out his Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons will dream dreams, though of immature age, since prophecy failed in the second temple. And the Holy of Holies is to be anointed with the oil of unction, since this oil failed in the second temple." Menasseh Ben Israel (De Termino Vitae, book III, section VI, §VI, "Seventy weeks," etc.) agrees almost entirely. Here present liberty is announced to him, and a future, new and harsh captivity of the people at some time, through which Israel would be cleansed from all guilt of sins. And after a brief interval he continues:

units.la: C interjectis ita pergit. Itaque cum dicit, decisa super populum ad consumendum prævaricationem iniquitatem & peccata, tantum est, quasi diceret, post consummationem CCCCXC. annorum sequetur ea populi tui captivitas, qua purgabitur ab idololatria, homicidio & adulterio, quæ sunt tria maxima peccata. Et post peractam hanc mundationem sequetur tempus Justitiæ, juxta illud, & ad adducendam Justitiam seculi, id est, non erit amplius peccatum, sed ut Jesaias ait Cap. LI. 8. Justitia erit semper. Alibi item Cap. x. 21. Et populus tuus omnis erit justus. Atque idem omnes attestantur Prophetæ. Subdit porro Daniel, ad sigillandum visionem & Prophetam, quasi diceret omnes Prophetiæ tum obsignabuntur, quatenus ea omnes, quæ futura erant, complebuntur. Vel ea Prophetæ mens, tum auctiorem fore vim Prophetiæ. Quippe Deus apud Joël ait, effundam Spiritum &c. Præterea ait, ad ungendum Sanctitatem Sanctitatum, id est Sanctum Sanctorum. Nam in secundo templo non fuit unctum, quia non foret æternum. Et post hæc vult dicere Propheta, finita Prophetia & Sacrificia instaurabuntur, quibus hodierno die caremus. Hæc Menasseh.
units.tr: Thus when he says, "a decision has been made concerning your people to bring an end to transgression, iniquity and sin," it is as if he said: after the completion of 490 years will follow that captivity of your people by which it will be purged of idolatry, homicide and adultery, which are the three greatest sins. And after this cleansing has been accomplished there will follow a time of righteousness, according to that saying, "and to bring in everlasting righteousness," that is, there will be no more sin, but, as Isaiah says in chapter 51:8, "Righteousness will be forever." Elsewhere likewise, chapter 60:21, "And your people will all be righteous." All the prophets bear witness to the same.
