Daniel further adds, "to seal up the vision and the prophet," as if he said that all prophecies will then be sealed, in so far as all that was to come will be fulfilled. Or the prophet's meaning is that then the power of prophecy will be greater. Indeed God says through Joel, "I will pour out my Spirit," etc. Furthermore he says, "to anoint the Holy of Holies," that is, the Holy of Holies. For in the second temple it was not anointed, because it would not be eternal. And after this the prophet wishes to say that, prophecy having ended, the sacrifices will be restored, which we lack today. Thus Menasseh.

units.la: XVII. Observamus primò generatim contra has Judaicas Glossas 1. Male finem LXX. Septimanarum poni ab ipsis in ultimo per Romanos excidio; qui error eo crassior est, quod simul initium habdomadum statuant in destructione ædis primæ per Chaldæos. 11. Non post finitas hebdomadas, sed intra illarum spatium, hæc evenire debuisse. Ideo enim hæ septimanæ populo restituto & urbi Sancta instauratæ concessæ erant, ut apud eum, ac in eâ, bona hæc adducerentur.
units.tr: XVII. We observe first, in general, against these Jewish glosses: (1) they wrongly place the end of the seventy weeks at the final destruction by the Romans, an error all the grosser because at the same time they fix the beginning of the weeks at the destruction of the first temple by the Chaldeans; (2) these things ought to have happened not after the weeks were finished, but within the span of those weeks. For those weeks were granted to the restored people and the restored holy city so that these good things might be brought to them, and among them.

units.la: XVIII. Secundo speciatim, & quidem quantum ad verba priora, ad peccatorum ablationem spectantia, dicimus, audacter Menasseh cum Abarbenele restringere peccata expianda ad idololatriam, homicidium, & adulterium vel incestus; cum tamen Angelus indefinite loquatur. Nec cohærent hæc verba Menasseh cum iis, quæ antea dixerat de Israëlis mundatione ab omni peccatorum reatu. Melius Jachiades omnia heic peccata oris operis & cogitationis intellexit. Videtur & huic Menasseæ exegesi subesse hæc erroris ἀπόφασις, quod על השגיאות propter errores & leviora peccata exitii rei non fuissent; & quod hodie nullo modo peccatis illis patrum consentiant, iisque suf-frafragentur, sed ob patrum peccata tantum poenas luant contra, Ezech. XVIII. 2. 3. Certe dissimulat uterque veram exilii hujus causam, quae est, quod Filium exosculati non fuerint Psal. II. 12. Rupem salutis יגבלי contumelijs affecerint, ut stultum ac improbum נבל tractaverint, imo נבלה Cadaver fecerint Deut. XXXII. 16. Jehovah צבאות factus למקדש in Sanctuarium, per assumtionem humanae naturae, in qua ἐσκήνωσε ut in Templo ac Tabernaculo habitavit inter homines Joh. I. 14. ipsis fuerit lapis offensionis & rupes scandali Isai. VIII. 14. 15. & quod Messiam principem occiderint v. 26. 27. Triplici porro adhibito verbo כלא / חהם / כפר ablationem reatus solam Menasseh, Iachiades vero etiam abolitionem maculae, ipsiusque peccandi actus, exprimi credit. Hic quidem male, si absolutam ἀναμαρτησίαν, quae in hac mortali vita nunquam est expectanda 1 Reg. VIII. 46. Eccles. VII. 20. his in verbis intelligat, nec peccabit amplius domus Israël. Ambo autem pertinaciter errant in eo, quod expiationem hanc promissam per hodiernam captivitatem duram, longeque extensam, absolvendam velint. Hoc quidem neutiquam dicit Angelus, nec dicerent hi Judaei, nisi animum divino judicio contra veritatem obdurassent. Aliter certe veteres Judaei, qui juxta relationem Menasseh haec verba, ad consummandum praevaricationem, ita exposuerunt, ut post expirationem LXX. hebdomadam, & adventum Messiae, peccata remitterentur. Haec recte se habent; peccatorum remissionem petierat Daniel, eam & annunciare debuit Angelus, siquidem preces ipsius exauditae essent, uti supponunt quoque hi Judaei; quod & facit his verbis, promittens remissionem actu promerendam sanguine Messiae excidendi, absque quo ἡ γίνεται ἀφεσις. Nec solum scopus & occasio hujus Prophetiae, sed & contextus, & verba ipsa, & rei natura, & analogia legis & Prophetarum palam Judaeis refragantur. Quae singula paucis ostendemus.
units.tr: XVIII. Secondly, in particular, and indeed as regards the earlier words, which concern the removal of sins, we say that Menasseh, boldly along with Abarbanel, restricts the sins to be atoned for to idolatry, murder, and adultery or incest; yet the angel speaks indefinitely. Nor do these words of Menasseh agree with what he had said before about Israel's cleansing from all guilt of sin. Jachiades understood all sins here better, as sins of the mouth, of the deed and of the thought. It seems that this interpretation of Menasseh is also underpinned by this denial of error, that on account of errors and lesser sins the exile would not have been brought about; and that today they in no way agree with those sins of the fathers, nor do they vote for them, but they suffer punishment only for the sins of the fathers, contrary to Ezek. 18:2, 3. Certainly both conceal the true cause of this exile, which is that they did not kiss the Son, Ps. 2:12; they treated the Rock of salvation [יגבלי] with contumely, handled him as a foolish and wicked man [נבל], and indeed made him a corpse [נבלה], Deut. 32:16. The LORD of hosts [צבאות] made into the sanctuary [למקדש], by the assumption of human nature, in which he tabernacled, dwelling among men as in a temple and tabernacle, John 1:14, became for them a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence, Isa. 8:14, 15; and they killed the Messiah the prince, v. 26, 27. Moreover, by the threefold use of the words [כלא / חהם / כפר], Menasseh believes that only the removal of guilt is expressed, but Jachiades that the abolition of the stain and of the very act of sinning is also expressed. Here Menasseh errs, if he understands by these words, the house of Israel will sin no more, an absolute sinlessness, which is never to be expected in this mortal life, 1 Kings 8:46, Eccles. 7:20. But both obstinately err in wishing this promised expiation to be completed by the present harsh captivity, which has been drawn out so long. The angel by no means says this, nor would these Jews say it, unless they had hardened their minds against the truth by divine judgment. The ancient Jews certainly interpreted these words, to finish the transgression, otherwise, according to Menasseh's report, namely that after the end of the seventy weeks and the coming of the Messiah sins would be forgiven. This is correct: Daniel had asked for the forgiveness of sins, and the angel ought to announce it, since his prayers were to be heard, as these Jews also assume; and he does so in these words, promising a remission to be actually obtained by the blood of the Messiah who is to be cut off, without which there is no ἄφεσις. Not only the aim and occasion of this prophecy, but also the context, the words themselves, the nature of the matter, and the analogy of the law and the prophets openly contradict the Jews. We shall show these points one by one in a few words.

units.la: XIX. Testatur Angelus v. 22. se prodiisse ut Danielem imbueret intelligentia.
units.tr: XIX. The angel testifies at v. 22 that he came forth to imbue Daniel with understanding.

units.la: Ipse Iachiades ad verba illa v. 23. בין כדבר hanc institutit paraphrasin, qua propter בין כדבר המפרש אשר אומר intellige verbum planum, explicitum, clarum, quod loquar. Minime vero sensu Judaico accepta haec verba sunt clara plana & exposita, & apta ad intelligentiam dandam Danieli. Imo potius quodvis aliud ex oeclusione, finitione, expiatione, peccati cogitare ipsi promptum erat, quam Israelis atroci hac calamitate punitionem horrendam. Etenim poenas exigens Deus plane contrariis phrasibus describitur in sacris, ut quod peccatum visitet, revelet, peccatori ob oculos ordine disponat, sibi ac lumini faciei suae proponat, ejusque recordetur &c. Exod. xx. 5. Thren. iv. 22. Psal. xxi. xc. 8. Hos. ix. 9. E contra remissio peccatorum penè iisdem & similibus phrasibus exprimitur, quales sunt peccatum non intueri, tegere, in profundum maris abjicere, removere, ejusque non recordari &c. Num. xxiii. 25. Ps. xxxii. 1. Mich. vii. 19. Zach. iii. 9. Ier. xxxi. 34. Et ne cavillentur Judaei, peccata heic non dici occludenda, obsignanda, uti nos vertimus, sed finienda, consummanda juxta aliam lectionem & interpretationem, de qua mox uberius, scire oportet, etiam hac phrasi remissionem peccati poenaeque ablationem significari in sacris, eamque opponi visitationi iniquitatis ac propter eam punitioni. Thren. iv. 22. consumta, finita est iniquitas tua, o filia Tzion, non perget in deportatione relinquere te: visitabit tuam iniquitatem o filia Edom, reteget peccata tua, vel deportabit te propter peccata tua. Utique expiare peccatum non potest notare, punire ipsum peccatorem & sontem pro insonte non habere, provenit enim ex misericordia divina, & ubique in scriptura irae divinae ac perditioni ipsius peccatoris opponitur Ps. lxxviii. 38. &c. Neutiquam ergo verbum planum & expositum satis exhibet heic Angelus, si id dicere voluerit, quod Judaei contendunt. Deinde rei natura quoque non patitur ut hodierna gentis calamitas peccati sui, patrumque suorum, sit expiatio. Nihil enim Lex habet de expiatione peccati propter poenam, vel afflictionem quamcunque temporalem, sed poenam imponit aeternam, absolutamque omnibus numeris maledictionem denunciat Deut. xxvii. 13. 26. & merito, quoniam infinitae majestatis laesionem non nisi infinito supplicio puniri, aequum est. Nullus ergo homo sibi persuadeat unquam, se pretium redemtionis pro anima sua vel etiam aliena Deo solvere posse. Vir fratrem redimendo non redimet nec dabit Deo redemtionis ejus pretium, & quare non, pretio & pondere nimis grave est enim, redemtionis illud pretium anianima eorum, quod si ab homine ipso solvi deberet, cessaret in seculum Pf. xlix. 8. 9. Ego, Ego ipse deleo defectiones tuas propter me, למעני / & peccatorum tuorum non recordor, dicit ideo Jehovah Ies. xliii. 22. Et nisi dudum à Lege defecissent Judæi, ex illius analogia proculdubio didicissent hanc suam captivitatem esse non posse expiationem peccatorum patrum. Docet enim Lex, quod qui ipse reus sit pro alterius reatu intervenire non possit, idque præsertim in summo Pontifice, quem debito prius exsolutum voluit Deus, antequam provinciam exsolvendi debito populum suscIperet Levit. xvi. 6. 11. Præterea juxta legem nulla erat expiatio peccati, nisi per sacrificium, & sanguinis fusionem. Nam sanguis ille, qui est nempe in altari, pro anima expiabit Levit. xvii. 11. Unde & Paulus benè eruditus in lege pronunciat; Et omnia fere juxta legem sanguine purificantur, καὶ χωρὶς αἱματεκχυσίας ὁ γίνεται ἄφεσις Heb. ix. 22. Nec diffitentur hoc Judæi vulgò; interrogati enim de causa diuturni hujus exilii, respondent, ideò se hactenus restitutos non esse, quia carent hostia & sacrificio ob defectum loci legitimi, quod unicum esset iram Dei sedandi medium. Ita juxta Origenem ab ævo locuti sunt. Quod dum faciunt, rectè agnoscunt se indigere victima piaculari, quæ coram irato ob scelera Numine vices eorum in subeundis pœnis suppleat. In eo autem perniciosè errant, quod vim expiandi brutorum animalium sanguini deputent, cum ille olim nil, nisi τῆς σαρκὸς καθαρότητα, effecerit, & veram animarum purificationem meliori & unico infiniti valoris sacrificio Filii Dei peragendam credentibus obsignaverit; hinc singulis diebus & solenniter quotannis fundebatur rursus, irrefragabili indicio illum ad animas haudquaquam sufficere purificandas. Unde & Deus per sedecim & amplius secula fundi sanguinem ad altare noluit, postquam verus Pontifex cum proprio sanguine cœleste sanctuarium ingressus est. Accedit tandem analogia prophetiarum, quibus frequenter Israeli mundatio peccatorum promittitur post captivitatem Babylonicam expectanda Ier. xxxi. 34. l. 18. 19. 20. Ezech. xxxvi. 25. 26. 29. Zach. iii. 9. In hisce & similibus locis promittit Deus Israeli mundationem à peccatis, & quidem absque ulla ejus recognitione, aut judiciali inquisitione, dum considerarentur, quasi non existerent; & quidem per adspersionem aqua munda super ip-sum, & non propter plagarum sine fine in ipsum immissionem; imo quod non prætereundum, se iniquitatem terra illius è conspectu suo remoturum testatur Deus uno die, vera sc. expiationis nunquam repetendo; non ergò per plures annos, multo minus per plura secula, sed die unico apparitionis veri sacerdotis, oblationis sui ipsius, ac ingressus in Sanctuarium cœleste. Hæc ergo captivitas non est expiatio peccati Israelis, sic enim ejus recordaretur certe Deus in ira, sic quæreret & inveniret cum judicio, neque sic aqua munda, pura, grata, refocillante, sed turbulentis iræ suæ rivis purgaret Israelem, & tandem non uno die, sed continuo repetito in plurimis invicem succedentibus generationibus ac seculis, Israelis iniquitatem removeret. Quid ergo? an fefellit Deus populum suum, prædicando pacem, cum gladius ad animam pertingeret? Absit hoc à fidelissimo Numine! sed falluntur & fallunt hi Judæi, dum ante notatas Prophetias & hanc nostram ita explicant, quasi ad totum Israelem, etiam incredulum, pertinerent, cum tamen non omnes, qui ex Israele sunt, Israel sint, & hæ prophetiæ verum Israelem & genuinos filios Abrahæ tantum respiciant. Hujus autem observationis negleƐtus fons erroris Judaici est, ut sibi stulte persuadeant, hodiernum exilium esse mundationem à peccatis heic à Daniele promissam.
units.tr: Jachiades himself, on the words of v. 23, gave this paraphrase: wherefore [בין כדבר המפרש אשר אומר] understand the word plain, explicit, clear, which I shall speak. Yet those words are by no means clear, plain and set out in the Jewish sense, or fit for giving Daniel understanding. Rather, it was more ready for him to think of any other meaning, such as closing off, ending, expiation of sin, than of the dreadful punishment of Israel by this atrocious calamity. For God, when exacting penalties, is described in the sacred writings by quite opposite phrases: that he visits sin, reveals it, sets it in order before the eyes of the sinner, sets it before himself and the light of his face, and remembers it, etc. Exod. xx. 5. Thren. iv. 22. Psal. xxi. xc. 8. Hos. ix. 9. On the contrary, forgiveness of sins is expressed almost by the same and similar phrases, such as not looking upon sin, covering it, casting it into the depths of the sea, removing it, and not remembering it, etc. Num. xxiii. 25. Ps. xxxii. 1. Mich. vii. 19. Zach. iii. 9. Ier. xxxi. 34. And lest the Jews cavil that sins are not here said to be shut up or sealed, as we translate, but finished, brought to an end, according to another reading and interpretation, of which more presently, one should know that even by this phrase the remission of sin and the removal of punishment are signified in the sacred writings, and it is set against the visitation of iniquity and the punishment on account of it. Thren. iv. 22: Your iniquity, O daughter of Zion, is consumed and finished; he will no longer carry you into exile: he will visit your iniquity, O daughter of Edom, he will uncover your sins, or he will carry you away for your sins. Certainly to expiate sin cannot mean to punish the sinner himself and to hold the guilty as innocent; for it comes from divine mercy, and everywhere in Scripture it is opposed to the wrath of God and the destruction of the sinner himself, Ps. lxxviii. 38, etc. Therefore by no means does the plain and expounded word present here the angel sufficiently, if he wished to say what the Jews contend. Next, the nature of the thing also does not allow the present calamity of the nation to be an expiation of its own sin and that of its fathers. For the Law says nothing of expiating sin by punishment or any temporal affliction whatever, but imposes eternal punishment and declares a curse absolute in every respect, Deut. xxvii. 13, 26, and rightly, since it is fair that an offence against infinite majesty be punished only with infinite suffering. Let no man therefore persuade himself that he can ever pay to God a price of redemption for his own soul, or even for another's. A man will not redeem his brother, nor give to God the price of his redemption; and why not? The price of the redemption of their soul is too heavy, by price and weight; it would cease for ever, Ps. xlix. 8, 9. I, I myself blot out your transgressions for my own sake, [למעני] and I do not remember your sins, says Jehovah, Isa. xliii. 22. And unless the Jews had long ago fallen away from the Law, they would undoubtedly have learned from its analogy that this captivity of theirs cannot be an expiation of the sins of the fathers. For the Law teaches that one who is himself guilty cannot intervene for another's guilt, and this especially in the high priest, whom God wished to be first freed from his own debt before he undertook the office of freeing the people from theirs, Levit. xvi. 6, 11. Moreover, according to the law there was no expiation of sin except through sacrifice and the shedding of blood. For that blood which is in the altar will make atonement for the soul, Levit. xvii. 11. Whence also Paul, well taught in the law, declares: And almost all things are purified by blood according to the law, and without shedding of blood there is no remission [καὶ χωρὶς αἱματεκχυσίας οὐ γίνεται ἄφεσις], Heb. ix. 22. Nor do the Jews commonly deny this; for when asked the reason for this long exile, they answer that they have not so far been restored because they lack victim and sacrifice, owing to the lack of the lawful place, which was the one means of appeasing God's anger. So they have spoken from the age of Origen. In doing so they rightly acknowledge that they need a victim of atonement, which before an angry Deity, on account of crimes, would stand in for them in undergoing punishments. In this, however, they err destructively, in that they attribute to the blood of brute animals the power of expiating, since that blood formerly effected nothing but the cleansing of the flesh [τῆς σαρκὸς καθαρότητα], and it sealed the true purification of souls, to be accomplished for believers by the better and unique sacrifice of infinite worth of the Son of God. Hence it was poured out again daily and yearly with solemn rites, an irrefutable sign that it was in no way sufficient to cleanse souls. Whence also God, for sixteen and more centuries, did not wish blood to be poured out at the altar, after the true High Priest entered the heavenly sanctuary with his own blood. Lastly there is the analogy of the prophecies, in which the cleansing of Israel from sins is frequently promised, to be looked for after the Babylonian captivity, Ier. xxxi. 34; l. 18, 19, 20; Ezech. xxxvi. 25, 26, 29; Zach. iii. 9. In these and similar passages God promises Israel cleansing from sins, and indeed without any acknowledgment or judicial inquiry, as if they did not exist; and indeed by sprinkling clean water upon them, not on account of plagues poured on them without end. Nay, what must not be passed over: God testifies that he will remove the iniquity of that land from his sight in one day, a true expiation, never to be repeated; not therefore over many years, much less over many centuries, but in one day, the day of the appearing of the true priest, of his own offering, and of his entry into the heavenly sanctuary. This captivity, therefore, is not an expiation of Israel's sin. For thus God would surely remember it in wrath; thus he would seek and find it with judgment; nor would he cleanse Israel with clean, pure, pleasing, refreshing water, but with the turbulent streams of his wrath; and at last, not in one day but by a continual repetition through many successive generations and centuries, he would remove Israel's iniquity. What then? Did God deceive his people, preaching peace when the sword reached the soul? Far be this from the most faithful Deity! But these Jews are deceived, and deceive, when they explain the prophecies noted above and this one of ours as if they pertained to all Israel, even the unbelieving, whereas not all who are of Israel are Israel, and these prophecies regard only the true Israel and the genuine sons of Abraham. The source of the Jewish error is the neglect of this observation, so that they foolishly persuade themselves that the present exile is the cleansing from sins promised here by Daniel.

units.la: XX. Reliqua tria Angeli effata in bonam partem sumunt Judæi, sed in omnibus non eodem modo explicant. Quantum ad adductionem justitiæ seculorum, inepte Jachiades per עולמים secula, domum æternam tertiam adhuc sc. extruendam, & per Justitiam הלוחות tabulas sc. legis, in illud Sanctuarium restituendas inferendas rursus, intelligit. Nullibi tabularum harum restitutionem pollicetur Deus, imo potius earum loco legem mentis suorum inditurum se, cordiqve eorum inscripturum, temporibus Messiæ testatur Jer. xxxi. 33. Hebraæ phrasi convenientius, Justitia seculorum, Justitia æterna, seu virtus justitiæ, in secula colenda, esse statuitur à Menasseh, cujus verba sunt. Et ad adducendam justitiam seculi, idest, non erit amplius peccatum, sed ut Jesaias ait, justitia erit semper Jes. i. 1. 8. Alibi item, & populus tuus omnis erit justus Jes. lx. 21. Atque idem omnes attestantur Prophetæ. Loquuntur quidem Prophetæ. phetæ de Justitia consummatissima, non in hominibus, sed in Germine Davidis, quæ imputanda iis, qui ipsum vocarent יהוה צרקנו Ier. xxiii. 5.6. Et de hac disserit loco priori Ief. li. 8. ipse servus Jehovæ, plenissime justificatus, (Cap. l. 3.) וצרקתי sed justitia mea in seculum erit, וישועתי & salus mea, fructus justitiæ meæ, per quam acquisita est, in generationem generationum. Promittunt porro iidem egregium augmentum cognitionis, sanctitatis, gaudii, tempore Messiæ conspiciendum in fidelibus, dum omni conatu ad perfectionem in cælis reservatam, adspirant. Et de hac inchoata quidem, sed eximia electorum post Christum sanctimonia in cælo plene consummanda, loquitur Iefaias cap. lx. 21. Et populus tuus, כלם universitas eorum, id est, omnes pariter justi erunt. Non video certè quomodo hæc ἀναμαρτησία Israelis, quam tempore Messiæ in hisce terris expectant Judæi, stare possit cum ipsorum hypothesibus de sacrificiis tum quoque instaurandis, ac libero arbitrio. Si enim nullum tum erit peccatum, quare ergo sacrificia mactabuntur, quæ utique Deus ad expiationem præcipue instituit olim. Et si impeccabiles plane futuri sunt, ubi est ergo indifferentiæ libertas? Et si actio timoris Dei non pendet à Deo tanquam necessarius effectus à causa suprema manans, sed tanquam effectus liber à causa libera, seu voluntate hominis libere agente producendus, uti loquitur Menasseh Lib. iii. Sect. viii. quomodo Deus heic & alibi se ab Israelitis perfecte colendum esse certò prædicere potest? Non est dicendum in rebus ipsis carumque fatali nexu hæc videre Deum, quorsum tendunt, quæ habet Menasseh Lib. iii. Cap. xi. sic enim lata ad Atheismum via sternitur: sed in liberrimo decreto suo de producendis talibus effectis infallibiliter cernere eum isthæc.
units.tr: XX. The Jews take the remaining three sayings of the angel in a good sense, but they do not explain them all in the same way. As to bringing in the righteousness of the ages, Jachiades foolishly understands by [עולמים] ages a third house, still to be built and eternal, and by righteousness [הלוחות] the tables of the law, to be restored and carried back into that sanctuary. Nowhere does God promise the restoration of these tables; rather, in their place he testifies, in the times of the Messiah, that he will put his law in the minds of his people and write it on their hearts, Jer. xxxi. 33. More suitably to the Hebrew idiom, righteousness of the ages, eternal righteousness, or the power of righteousness to be cultivated for ever, is affirmed by Menasseh, whose words are: And to bring in the righteousness of the age, that is, there will be no more sin; but, as Isaiah says, righteousness will always be, Jes. i. 1, 8. Elsewhere likewise: and all your people will be righteous, Jes. lx. 21. And all the Prophets attest the same. The Prophets indeed speak of the most consummate righteousness, not in men but in the Branch of David, which is to be imputed to those who call him Jehovah our righteousness, Ier. xxiii. 5, 6. And of this the servant of Jehovah himself, most fully justified (chap. 50.3), speaks in Isa. li. 8: [וצרקתי] but my righteousness will be for ever, [וישועתי] and my salvation, the fruit of my righteousness, by which it was obtained, to generation after generation. The same prophets further promise an outstanding increase of knowledge, holiness and joy, to be seen in the faithful in the time of the Messiah, while they strive with every effort toward the perfection reserved in heaven. And of this begun but outstanding sanctity of the elect after Christ, to be fully completed in heaven, Isaiah speaks in chap. lx. 21: And your people, [כלם] all of them, that is, all alike will be righteous. I certainly do not see how this sinlessness of Israel, which the Jews expect in these lands in the time of the Messiah, can stand together with their own hypotheses about sacrifices then to be restored, and about free will. For if there will then be no sin, why will sacrifices be slaughtered, which God chiefly instituted of old for atonement? And if they are to be wholly impeccable, where then is the freedom of indifference? And if the action of the fear of God does not depend on God as a necessary effect flowing from a supreme cause, but as a free effect to be produced by a free cause, that is, by the will of man acting freely, as Menasseh, Lib. iii. Sect. viii, speaks, how can God here and elsewhere be certain beforehand that he will be perfectly worshipped by the Israelites? It must not be said that God sees these things in the things themselves and their fatal connection, toward which those things tend, as Menasseh has it in Lib. iii. Cap. xi; for thus a road to atheism is laid open. Rather he sees them infallibly in his most free decree concerning the production of such effects.

units.la: XXI. Obsignationem visionis & Prophetæ explicat Jachiades ex Joel ii. 28.
units.tr: XXI. Jachiades explains the sealing of the vision and of the prophet from Joel 2:28.

units.la: uti etiam Menasseh, quasi sensus foret, majorem fore vim Prophetiæ, Spiritusque Prophetici in hominibus quibuscunque. Sed apparet visionem & Prophetam non in genere donum Prophetiæ, sed extantia modo Prophetarum oracula de rebus futuris significare. Præterea obsignandi vocabulo inest quidem virtutis cujusdam notio, sed talis, quæ non ad personas prophetantes, sed ad eorum dicta ac scripta referri debet. Hæc enim sigillo vim ac firmitatem accipere solent. Et si obsigna-tio tio hæc ad prophetiæ donum respiceret, verius ejus ablatio- nem, quam incrementum diceret. Unde & Menasseh, parum huic exegesi fidens, alteram præmittit de impletione eorum, quæ prophetæ prædixerunt. Quæ recte se haberent, nisi hanc impletionem prophetiæ post finitam hanc captivitatem rejiceret Judæus; cum nil fere restet implendum, nisi ea, quæ de conversione Judæorum ad dudum natum Messiam prædixêre Vates.
units.tr: as Menasseh also does, as if the meaning were that there would be a greater power of prophecy, and of the prophetic Spirit, in men of every kind. But it is clear that the vision and the prophet signify not the gift of prophecy in general, but the oracles of the prophets concerning future things that still survive. Moreover, the word sealing does carry some notion of a certain power, but one that must be referred not to the prophesying persons but to their sayings and writings, since seals usually give force and firmness to things. And if this sealing referred to the gift of prophecy, it would more truly speak of its removal than of its increase. Hence Menasseh, having little confidence in this interpretation, puts forward another, about the fulfilment of what the prophets foretold. This would be well and good, were it not that the Jew rejects this fulfilment of prophecy after the end of this captivity, since almost nothing remains to be fulfilled except what the seers foretold concerning the conversion of the Jews to the Messiah, long since born.

units.la: XXII. Quæ Judæi ad ultimam hujus versus pericopam commentantur, nituntur vulgari illa apud ipsos hypothesi de Templo Tertio, quod ædificandum adhuc, atque ungendum foret in signum perpetuitatis suæ, & in supplementum defectus, qui fuit sub Templo Secundo.
units.tr: XXII. What the Jews comment on the last clause of this verse rests on their common hypothesis about a Third Temple, which is yet to be built and to be anointed, as a sign of its perpetuity and as a supplement to the deficiency that existed under the Second Temple.

units.la: Quam hypothesin vanam esse paucis dicam. Scilicet eam rerum faciem, diebus Messiæ futuram, depingunt Prophetæ, quæ Templum materiale, omnemque Mosaicum cultum plane destruit. Omnes gentes venirent & incurvarent se coram Domino Ps. LXXXVI. 9. quas utique nullum materiale Templum caperet. Omni in loco Deo munera offerrent & suffimenta adolerent, ab ortu solis ad ejus occasum usque Mal. 1. 11. Altare Jehova haberet in media terra Ægypti Jes. XIX. 19. Præterea Omnisufficiens Omnipræsens & Spiritualis Numinis natura non patitur, ut ipsi ædes lapidea extruatur, ea habitaculum ejus nuncupetur, ac in ea ipsi cultus corporeus deferatur, nisi subsit mysterium & adumbratio rei altioris Jes. LXVI. 1. Act. VII. 48. 42. Qualis mystica præfiguratio Messiæ cum fuerit olim in Templo, hoc tam diu conservavit incolume Deus, donec umbram corpus dispelleret, ac Christus promissus appareret. Quo facto statim ostendit, totali urbis & Templi interitu, quod Numini altissimo in ædé manufacta habitare indecens esset & indignum. Et quoniam spes Judæorum de Templo Tertio nititur opinione æternæ obligationis, quæ est in institutis cerimoniis Mosaicis, ob quam adeo hæ olim, una cum Templo, reducendæ sint, apparet, si cerimonias ad tempus modo injunctas fuisse adstrui queat, hanc eorum expectationem Tertii cujusdam Templi, cum cerimoniis arctissimum nexum habentis, vanam esse & insipidam. Hujus autem veritatis, uti dari possent plurima irrefragabilia argumenta, ita nos unico hoc ratiocinio contenti erimus. Res animadmadversione digna est, quod Deus nullibi sacrificia offerri voluerit, quam in loco, quem elegerat, Templo scil. Hierosolymitano. Hujus autem à tot seculis eversio, novaque tentata per Julianum, sed insigni miraculo impedita restauratio, argumentum exhibet, quod maƈtatio pecudum & aromatum suffimenta ad essentiam religionis non speƈtent, sed veræ fidei & pietatis exercitamenta corporalia, & Ecclesiæ infantilis statui approportionata, fuerint, adeoque etiam ad adultiorem usque ætatem modo injunƈta. Cæteroquin enim locum hisce peragendis destinatum non extirpasset Deus, vel ad eum unice illa non adstrinxisset, atque populum suum necessariis religionis aƈtibus seque ipsum principali sibique placente cultu sine fine & termino non orbasset.
units.tr: I will say briefly that this hypothesis is empty. The state of affairs that the prophets depict for the days of the Messiah utterly destroys a material Temple and the whole Mosaic worship. All nations shall come and bow down before the Lord (Ps. LXXXVI. 9), which no material Temple could contain. In every place they shall offer gifts to God and burn incense, from the rising of the sun to its setting (Mal. 1. 11). There shall be an altar to Jehovah in the midst of the land of Egypt (Isa. XIX. 19). Moreover, the nature of the all-sufficient, omnipresent and spiritual Deity does not allow a house of stone to be built for him, to be called his dwelling, and bodily worship to be offered to him in it, unless some mystery and adumbration of a higher reality lies behind it (Isa. LXVI. 1; Acts VII. 48, 42). Whatever mystical prefiguration of the Messiah there once was in the Temple, God kept it intact for so long, until the body dispelled the shadow and the promised Christ appeared. Once this had happened, he at once showed, by the total destruction of the city and the Temple, that it was unseemly and unworthy for the Most High to dwell in a house made by hands. And since the Jews' hope of a Third Temple rests on the opinion of an eternal obligation attached to the Mosaic ceremonies, on account of which these must be restored together with the Temple, it is apparent that if it can be shown that the ceremonies were enjoined only for a time, their expectation of a certain Third Temple, which has the closest bond with the ceremonies, is vain and foolish. Of this truth there could be very many irrefutable arguments, but we shall be content with this single line of reasoning. It is worth noting that God nowhere wished sacrifices to be offered except in the place he had chosen, namely the Temple at Jerusalem. The overthrow of that Temple for so many centuries, and the restoration attempted by Julian but prevented by a remarkable miracle, show that the slaughter of animals and the burning of incense did not belong to the essence of religion. They were bodily exercises of true faith and piety, fitted to the infant state of the Church, and so were enjoined only until a more mature age. Otherwise God would not have uprooted the place appointed for these acts, nor bound his worship to that place alone, nor deprived his people, without end or limit, of the necessary acts of religion and of himself, the principal and pleasing worship.

units.la: XXIII. Dolendum est, quod Judæis occæcatis jungere debeamus virum Christianum, qui æque ac illi, nihil heic de Christo videns, audaci instituto, nobile hoc contra Judæos vaticinium nobis eripit, atque ad suas hypotheses verba tantum non omnia absurdissimè lacerat, ac torquet; JOHANNEM MARSHAMUM puta, doƈtum ac nobilem Anglum, in Canon. Chron. ad Sec. XVIII. Supponit quatuor Danielis visiones, sex posterioribus Capitibus enarratas, non ultra Antiochi Epiphanis tempora procedere, atque unam eandemque rem, sed diversis modis indicare, sic ut prima secunda & quarta Historiam prænuncient, hæc autem tertia visio etiam Chronologiam exhibeat. Dispescit itaque totum vaticinium in duas partes. Prima continet ἀνάκλησιν eorum, quæ à Daniele petita sunt hoc Capite, atque promissionem de reditu Judæorum post septem hebdomadas, numerandas ab anno vastitatis Hierosolymitanæ vicesimo primo, quo exiit verbum, id est Angelus mandatum à Deo accepit, ut responderet Danieli de quæsitis. Pertinent ad hanc primam partem verba vers. 24. & priora illa vers. 25. Scito ergo & intellige. Ab exitu verbi, ad reverti faciendum & ad ædificandum Jerusalem, usque ad unƈtum Ducem, hebdomades VII. Altera pars continet revelationem novam de Templi prophanatione per Antiochum, futura post LXIII. hebdomadas cum dimidiâ, supputandas non ab reditu Judæorum, neque ab exitu verbi, sed abexcidio Templi Salomonici. Hæc a nobis eo fine referuntur, ut Lectori pateat, ex quo fonte profluat sequens, quam exhibemus, paraphrasis super ea, quæ præ manibus sunt, sex Angeli enunciata.
units.tr: XXIII. It is to be regretted that we must join to the blinded Jews a Christian man who, like them, sees nothing here about Christ. With a bold undertaking he snatches from us this noble prophecy against the Jews, and almost wholly tears and twists its words to suit his hypotheses, most absurdly. I mean JOHN MARSHAM, a learned and noble Englishman, in Canon. Chron. at Sec. XVIII. He supposes that the four visions of Daniel, narrated in the last six chapters, do not proceed beyond the time of Antiochus Epiphanes, and that they indicate one and the same thing in different ways, so that the first, second and fourth foretell history, while this third vision also exhibits chronology. He thus divides the whole prophecy into two parts. The first contains a recapitulation [ἀνάκλησις] of the things asked of Daniel in this chapter, and the promise of the return of the Jews after seven weeks, to be counted from the twenty-first year of the desolation of Jerusalem, when the word went forth, that is, when the angel received command from God to answer Daniel's questions. To this first part belong verse 24 and the earlier words of verse 25: Know therefore and understand. From the going forth of the word to restore and to build Jerusalem, unto the anointed Prince, seven weeks. The second part contains a new revelation of the profanation of the Temple by Antiochus, to come after sixty-three and a half weeks, to be reckoned not from the return of the Jews, nor from the going forth of the word, but from the destruction of Solomon's Temple. We set these things out so that the reader may see from what source flows the following paraphrase, which we give, of the six angelic announcements before us.

units.la: XXV. Hanc autem hunc in modum instituit. Ad consummandum prævaricationem. De prævaricatione Judæorum, qua prævaricati sunt in Deum, vide verf. 7. & deinceps. Sensus est: ut exilium, quo Deus puniit Judæorum contumaciam, finem accipiat. Vide 2 Reg. 24. 4. 5. Ad obsignandum peccata; Daniel peccata fassus est verf. 5. & deinceps. Sensus: ut peccatorum pœna finem habeat: Obsignari solent quæ completa sunt. Sic in computo Judaico, ad obsignatam Misna, ad obsignatum Talmud, id est, absolutum. Ad expiandum iniquitatem. Ut luatur iniquitas; ut avertat fe ira Dei verf. 16. ut condonet Deus, verf. 19. & Judæis reconcilietur. Ad adducendum Justitiam seculorum, Æternam, Dei scilicet: cui tribuitur Justitia ipsa verf. 7. & deprecatus est iram Dei contra Hierosolymam, fecundum omnes suas justitias verf. 16. Ad sigillandum visionem & Prophetiam. Ut impleatur Prophetia Jeremiæ de Captivitatis fine; qui in hac visione certo annorum numero, rursus confirmatur. Et adungendum sanctitatem sanctitatem. Templum & Sacerdotium Sancti Sanctorum titulo insigniuntur. Daniel questus est verf. 17. de Sanctuario Dei desolato. De unctione mox ad verf. 26. Apparet ex his, omnia hæc effata temporale & externum beneficium juxta ipsum continere, & impleri in reductione populi, solutione captivitatis, & reparatione Urbis & Sanctuarii ex Edicto & permissu Cyri Regis Persarum. Fundamentum porro hujus exegefios est, quod in his verbis fit ἀνάλνψις eorum, quæ à Daniele hoc capite petita sunt. Petiit autem pœnæ præfentis in exilio gravissimo, propter peccata populi inflictæ, remotionem, peccati adeoque remissionem, Urbisque ac Sanctuarii devastati reftaurationem.
units.tr: XXV. He sets it out in this way. To finish the transgression. On the transgression of the Jews, by which they transgressed against God, see verse 7 and following. The sense is that the exile, by which God punished the stubbornness of the Jews, should come to an end. See 2 Kings 24. 4, 5. To seal up sins. Daniel confessed the sins, verse 5 and following. The sense: that the punishment of sins should have an end. Things that are completed are usually sealed up. So in the Jewish reckoning the Mishnah is said to be sealed, and the Talmud sealed, that is, finished. To make atonement for iniquity. That iniquity may be paid for; that the wrath of God may be turned away, verse 16; that God may pardon, verse 19, and be reconciled to the Jews. To bring in everlasting righteousness, eternal, namely of God, to whom righteousness itself is ascribed, verse 7, and he besought the wrath of God against Jerusalem according to all his righteousnesses, verse 16. To seal up the vision and the prophecy. That the prophecy of Jeremiah concerning the end of the captivity may be fulfilled, which in this vision is confirmed again by a certain number of years. And to anoint the most holy. Temple and priesthood are marked by the title Holy of Holies. Daniel complained, verse 17, of the desolate sanctuary of God. On the anointing, soon, at verse 26. It appears from these things that, in his view, all these sayings contain a temporal and external benefit, and are fulfilled in the return of the people, the release from captivity, and the rebuilding of the city and sanctuary by the edict and permission of Cyrus, King of the Persians. The foundation of this exegesis is that in these words there is a recapitulation [ἀνάκλησις] of the things Daniel asked for in this chapter. He asked for the removal of the present punishment, the very grievous exile inflicted for the sins of the people, and so the removal of sin, and the restoration of the devastated city and sanctuary.

units.la: XXVI. Verum adversatur hæc exegesis 1. Verborum connexioni, quæ ita efferuntur ab Angelo, ut lxx. septimanas dicat decisas à Deo, eum in finem, ut consummetur prævaricatio &c. Absurde autem quadringentos nonaginta annos quis diceret constitutos ad negotium quoddam procurandum, quod intra quadraginta novem annos fieri debebat. Et restitutionem populi & urbis non esse finem, sed principium lxx. septimanarum, patebit ad v. 25. 11. Verborum emphasi amplitudini & & indefinitæ propositioni. Ubi Daniel sua & populi sui peccata confessus modo est, ac Angelus de populo & urbe definitè locutus, heic indefinite de peccatis defectione & iniquitate, non solius Danielis, non Judæorum tantum, sed omnium, ex quavis gente, electorum loquitur. Neque etiam Visionem hanc, aut Jeremiam Prophetam unum, sed in genere Visionem & Prophetam, sive Prophetiam quamcunque, collectivè, nominat. Et, quæso, an liberatio Judæorum ex captivitate corporali & externa, quæ verius pœnæ quædam dilatio, quam ablatio dicenda est, respectu potissimæ gentis illius partis, olim obdurandæ ac penitus extirpandæ per Romanos, dici potest, consummatio, obsignatio, expiatio peccatorum ejus? Etenim hæ phrases, ita multiplicatæ, non pœnæ cujusdam suspensionem, sed pœnæ omnis cum corporis tum animæ ablationem æternam notare debent, nisi eas emphasi sua privare velimus. Haud malè quidem, ut expietur iniquitas, interpretatur, ut luatur iniquitas. Luere enim iniquitatem is dicitur, qui debitas pœnas dat pro peccato, vel qui pœnas subeundo obligationem peccati ad pœnam solvit, vel qui peccatum satisfactione eluit ac tollit. Liberationem itaque à reatu, idque propter pœnam debitam perferendam Angelus sic promittit. Est ergo aliquis cogitandus, qui iniquitatem pœnas solvendo lueret. Populum Judaicum intendit Vir Doctus. Verum sic non promissionem, sed comminationem reperimus. Et cum consummare, obsignare peccatum, adducere justitiam &c. ad Deum referatur, temere certe & contra seriem sermonis, expiare seu luere iniquitatem populo tribuitur. Præterea antecedentia & consequentia effata in restitutione populi impleri contendit Vir Doctus; ergo & hoc de expiatione peccati. Quod etiam vult; sed ita, ut ad effectum expiationis & luitionis peccati, qui est aversio iræ divinæ ac Numinis reconciliatio, modo attendat; animadvertens facile ipsum τὸ expiare & luere iniquitatem, quod proprie pœnas dare pro peccato, atque hoc modo demum illius obligationem ad pœnam tollere, dicit, non posse locum habere, finita jam peccatorum pœna & captivitate tristi. Sed sic rursus proprietati emphasi & amplitudini verborum adversatur, quod ipsum fecisse contendimus.
units.tr: XXVI. But this exegesis is opposed, first, by the connection of the words, which the angel pronounces in such a way as to say that the seventy weeks were decreed by God to this end, that the transgression may be finished, and so on. Yet it would be absurd to say that four hundred and ninety years were set apart for the accomplishment of some business that ought to have been done within forty-nine years. And that the restoration of the people and the city is not the end but the beginning of the seventy weeks will be clear from verse 25. Second, it is opposed by the emphasis and breadth of the words, and by the indefinite form of the proposition. Where Daniel has just confessed his own sins and those of his people, and the angel has spoken definitely of the people and the city, here he speaks indefinitely of sins, defection and iniquity. He speaks collectively, not of this vision or of the one prophet Jeremiah, but of the vision and the prophet in general, or of any prophecy whatever. He speaks not of Daniel alone, nor of the Jews alone, but of all the elect from every nation. And I ask, can the liberation of the Jews from bodily and external captivity, which is more truly to be called a certain postponement of punishment than its removal, with respect to that principal part of that nation, destined to be hardened and utterly uprooted by the Romans, be called the consummation, sealing and expiation of its sins? For these phrases, piled up as they are, ought to signify not the suspension of some punishment but the eternal removal of all punishment, both of body and of soul, unless we wish to deprive them of their emphasis. Quite rightly he interprets that iniquity may be expiated as that iniquity may be paid for. For to pay iniquity is said of one who gives the due penalties for sin, or who, by undergoing penalties, discharges the obligation of sin to punishment, or who by satisfaction washes away and removes sin. So the angel promises liberation from guilt, and that on account of the penalty to be borne. Therefore someone must be thought of who would pay for iniquity by enduring penalties. The learned man means the Jewish people. But in this way we find not a promise but a threat. And since to finish, to seal up, to bring in righteousness and so on are referred to God, it is surely rash, and contrary to the run of the speech, to attribute to the people the expiating or paying for iniquity. Moreover, the learned man contends that the sayings before and after are fulfilled in the restoration of the people, and therefore this too, concerning the expiation of sin. He wants this as well; but only so far as he looks to the effect of expiation and payment for sin, which is the turning away of divine wrath and the reconciliation of the Deity. He notices that the very notion of expiating and paying for iniquity, which properly means giving penalties for sin and in this way at last removing the obligation to punishment, cannot have a place once the punishment is already finished and the sad captivity is over. But in this way he again opposes the proper emphasis and breadth of the words, which is exactly what we contend he has done.

units.la: XXVI. Incerti sumus, quid per justitiam æternam intelligat, quam explicandam vult ex v. 7. & 16. hujus Capitis, qui-bus
units.tr: XXVI. We are unsure what he means by "everlasting righteousness," which he wants explained from vv. 7 and 16 of this chapter, where the word "righteousness" is not used in the same way.

units.la: bus locis non eodem modo vox justitia capitur. Conjicio autem per justitiam eum intelligere benignitatem Numinis in reductione populi demonstrandam. Uti Versio Græca habet ad v. 16. ἡ ἐν πᾶσιν ἐλεημοσύνη σου. Sed cum illa fuerit temporaria, & Judæi rursus, post paucas annorum centurias, ejiciendi essent, æternam eam vix nuncupasset Angelus. Sanctitas quoque Sanctitatum ungenda, non potest esse Templum vel Sacerdotium, quia Sanctitas Sanctitatum, æque ac Dux & Excidendus, ob unctionis attributum, unum idemque, nempe personam aliquam singularem, non rem quandam, aut integrum hominum ordinem exprimere omnino dicenda est.
units.tr: I conjecture, however, that by "righteousness" he means the kindness of God to be shown in the restoration of the people. So the Greek version has at v. 16: "your mercy in all things" [ἡ ἐν πᾶσιν ἐλεημοσύνη σου]. But since that was temporary, and the Jews would again have to be cast out after a few centuries, the angel could hardly have called it "everlasting." Nor can the "Holy of Holies" to be anointed be the Temple or the priesthood, because "Holy of Holies," like "Prince" and "the one to be cut off," by the attribute of anointing, must be taken to express one and the same thing, namely some singular person, and not a thing or an entire order of men.

units.la: XXVII. Atqui, inquit Vir Doctus, ultra restitutionem populi & dissolutionem captivitatis non procedit Oratio Danielis; atque est in his verbis apertus respectus ad verba ejus, ac ἀνάληψις corum, quæ à Daniele petita sunt. Respondemus. 1. Integrum hoc vaticinium ostendit, plura Angelum & majora revelasse, quam quæ præcisè Daniel petierat. 11. Non desunt, qui opinantur, quod Daniel, pro dissolutione Captivitatis ac refectione Hierosolymæ orans, sub istis vocibus res majores, liberationem nempe spiritualem ex captivitate Diaboli & peccati intenderit, cujus hæc corporalis liberatio imago quædam ac documentum erat. 111. Fert consuetudo Spiritus Dei in Prophetis, ut de reversione Judæorum ex Babele loquens, tantum non ubique promissionem de redemtione spirituali per Christum jungat, cujus imago erat illa, atque cujus causa maximè fieri debebat. 1v. Verba Angeli, prodii ut imbuam te intelligentia v. 22. prodiit verbum ad quod indicandum venio, quia desideratissimus es, quapropter animadverte ipsum verbum, & intellige visionem v. 23. præ se ferunt indicationem mysterii cujusdam, hominibus cognitu apprimè necessarii, ex qua etiam Daniel intelligeret, se singulariter dilectum esse. Ergò majus quid & aliud hac prophetiâ & hisce verbis revelat Angelus, quam restitutionem populi Urbis ac Templi, aut ejus etiam novam prophanationem per Antiochum. Quæ certe mysterium tantum, tam sedulò inquirendum, & cujus indicatio esset ad dandam singularem intelligentiam, & signum eximii favoris divini erga Danielem, non continent. v. Falsum est, quod Danielis Oratio non procedat ultra liberationem ex captivitate BaBabylonica. Anhelat ille simul adventum Domini promissi, cujus gratia corporale hoc beneficium desiderat. Fac ut luceat facies tua super Sanctuarium Tuum, quod desolatum est, propter Dominum VI. . Denique singula verba hoc modo consbefore considerata pulcherrimum respectum habent ad verba Danielis. Hic peccata sua & suorum cuncta & multifaria fassus erat, & condonationem expetierat enixè. Angelus non solum condonationem particularem & remissionem poenæ præsentis, sed universalem omnium peccatorum expiationem & deletionem æternam sanguine Christi efficiendam promittit. Omnes suas Justitias abnegaverat prorsus Daniel. Rectè igitur Angelus Justitiam æternam consummatissimam à Christo adducendam prædicit. Implementum Prophetiæ Jeremiæ petierat Daniel. Angelus non hujus tantum, sed omnis Prophetiæ & visionis, de salute hominum per Christum acquirenda, confirmationem, per actualem impletionem, declarat esse futuram. Pro terrestri tandem Sanctuario supplicaverat Deo Daniel. Ipsum Jehovam Sanctuarium populi sui, & קדש קדשים fore, atque cum magno suorum gaudio ungendum prædicat Angelus. Sit itaque ἀνάλυψις eorum, quæ à Daniele petita sunt, in his verbis, id magis exegesi nostræ favebit, quam Viri Docti.
units.tr: XXVII. "But," says the learned man, "Daniel's prayer goes no further than the restoration of the people and the release from captivity, and in these words there is a clear reference back to his words and a taking up [ἀνάληψις] of what Daniel asked for." We reply. (1) This whole prophecy shows that the angel revealed more and greater things than what Daniel had precisely asked for. (2) There are those who think that Daniel, praying for the release from captivity and the rebuilding of Jerusalem, under these words intended greater things, namely spiritual liberation from the captivity of the Devil and of sin, of which this bodily liberation was a kind of image and pledge. (3) The custom of the Spirit of God in the Prophets is that, when speaking of the return of the Jews from Babylon, they almost everywhere join a promise of spiritual redemption through Christ, of which that return was an image, and for whose sake it was chiefly to take place. (4) The angel's words, "I came forth to instruct you in understanding" (v. 22), and "a word went forth, which I come to declare, for you are greatly beloved; therefore mark the word itself and understand the vision" (v. 23), carry the mark of some mystery, most necessary for men to know, by which Daniel too would understand that he was singularly beloved. So the angel reveals through this prophecy and these words something greater and other than the restoration of the people, the city and the Temple, or even its new profanation by Antiochus. These certainly do not contain a mystery so earnestly to be inquired into, whose indication would give singular understanding, and a sign of the extraordinary favour of God toward Daniel. (5) It is false that Daniel's prayer goes no further than deliverance from Babylonian captivity. At the same time he longs for the coming of the promised Lord, for whose sake he desires this bodily benefit: "Make your face shine upon your sanctuary, which is desolate, for the Lord's sake" (Dan. 9:17). Finally, the individual words, considered in this way, have a most beautiful relation to the words of Daniel. There he had confessed his own sins and those of his people, all and manifold, and earnestly sought forgiveness. The angel promises not only a particular forgiveness and remission of present punishment, but the universal expiation of all sins and their eternal blotting out, to be effected by the blood of Christ. Daniel had utterly renounced all his own righteousnesses, so rightly the angel foretells that the most perfect, eternal righteousness is to be brought in by Christ. Daniel had asked for the fulfilment of Jeremiah's prophecy. The angel declares that not only the confirmation of this prophecy, but of all prophecy and vision concerning the salvation of men to be obtained through Christ, will come about by actual fulfilment. Finally, Daniel had prayed to God for the earthly sanctuary. The angel foretells that Jehovah himself will be the sanctuary of his people, the Holy of Holies [קדש קדשים], and will be anointed with great joy on the part of his people. So the taking up of what Daniel asked for lies in these words, and this will favour our exegesis more than that of the learned man.

units.la: XXVIII. Non parum dissentit in explicatione verborum horum à reliquâ Interpretum turba præclarus Theologus Franciscus Junius. Summa hujus divini responsi juxta ipsum est; Deum populo indulgere LXX. Septimanas annorum, ut tempus gratiæ ac longanimitatis; hunc in finem, ut populus, adhuc in peccatis perseverans, resipiscat serio. Quod nisi fecerit, stare sententiam, & decisionem divinam, fore ut ἀμετα-μέλητῳ post spatium 490. annorum, præcise, justo Dei judicio perfundetur. Circumscribitur itaque tempus, ejusque terminus his verbis; LXX. Septimanæ decisæ sunt super populum tuum, & civitatem sanctam tuam. Finis autem hujus temporis in sequentibus. Hic duplex est; I. Ut resipiscat populus, malo renunciando, & bonum fide prehendendo II. Ut justa exercitamenta & media, ad resipiscentiam & fidem pertinentia, colat & observet. Quod renunciare malo populus debeat universe & singulariter, ostendit Deus his verbis, ad intercludendam defectionem, omnem, & ad obsignandum peccata, singula Bonorum vero profecutio in fide similiter duabus locutionibus ostenditur : particulariter, cum jubentur pii expiare iniquitatem, id est, Sacrificium illud ad expiationem efficax, quod est Christi Jesu, singuli exhibere Domino; & communiter sive universe, cum dicitur, & ad exhibendam Justitiam seculorum, id est, non temporariam aut humanam ullam, sed Justitiam Dei per fidem. Nam haec demum vera aeternaque est Justitia, qua justificamur coram Domino, & in aeternum accepti sumus. Ad hunc autem finem assequendum, quia nemo homo satis esse potest, Deus media quaedam instrumenta & signa instituit in Ecclesia sua, quorum adjumento Ecclesiam voluit in illa respipiscentia & fide Justitiaque aeterna stabilire. Ea adjumenta in Ecclesia Judaeorum fuerunt duum generum, nimirum Prophetia & cultus externus in Templo Dei Jerusalaimis, quae duo altera hujus versus parte Danieli exponuntur; prius his verbis, & ad obsignandum visionem & Prophetam, id est, ut singuli Prophetiam, cujus successionem gratiosam in Ecclesia sua aliturus est Deus, in mentibus suis obsignent, & ipsi a Deo eadem obsignentur: posterius illis, & ad ungendum locum Sanctum Sanctorum. Ubi, quantum ego percipio ex Viri Doctissimi verbis, ungere Sanctum Sanctorum ipsi notat, ordinario cultui in Templo vacare, sed in spiritu & veritate. Hactenus exegesin Magni Theologi expressimus, quantum fieri potuit brevitatis causa, etiam ipsius verbis.
units.tr: XXVIII. The distinguished theologian Franciscus Junius differs not a little from the rest of the interpreters in explaining these words. According to him, the sum of this divine answer is that God grants the people seventy weeks of years as a time of grace and long-suffering, to this end: that the people, still persisting in their sins, may repent seriously. If they do not, the decision and sentence of God stands, and it will come to pass that, after a span of exactly 490 years, they will be overwhelmed by the just judgment of God, which cannot be revoked [ἀμεταμέλητος]. The time is thus bounded, and its limit is marked by these words: "Seventy weeks are decreed upon your people and upon your holy city." The end of this time lies in what follows, and it is twofold: (1) that the people may repent, renouncing evil and laying hold of good by faith; (2) that they may cultivate and observe the just exercises and means pertaining to repentance and faith. That the people ought to renounce evil, both universally and individually, God shows in these words: "to stop transgression" (the whole), "and to seal up sins" (each single one). The pursuit of good in faith is likewise shown in two expressions: particularly, when the godly are bidden "to make atonement for iniquity," that is, each one is to offer to the Lord that sacrifice which is efficacious for expiation, namely Christ Jesus; and commonly or universally, when it is said, "and to bring in everlasting righteousness," that is, not a temporary or any human righteousness, but the righteousness of God through faith. For this alone is the true and eternal righteousness by which we are justified before the Lord and accepted for ever. To attain this end, since no man can be sufficient, God instituted certain means and signs in his Church, by whose help he willed the Church to be established in that repentance, faith and eternal righteousness. These helps in the Church of the Jews were of two kinds, namely prophecy and external worship in the Temple of God at Jerusalem. These two are set forth to Daniel in the other part of this verse: the former in the words "and to seal up vision and prophet," that is, that individuals should seal in their minds the prophecy whose gracious succession God will nourish in his Church, and that they themselves should be sealed by God in the same way; the latter in "and to anoint the Most Holy place." Here, as far as I perceive from the words of this most learned man, to anoint the Holy of Holies means to attend to the ordinary worship in the Temple, but in spirit and truth. Thus far I have set out the exegesis of this great theologian, as briefly as I could, and in his own words where possible.

units.la: XXIX. Fateor; haec mihi nimis conquisita videntur. Reponimus itaque.
units.tr: XXIX. I grant that these seem to me overly far-fetched. We reply, therefore, as follows.

units.la: 1. Oravit Daniel pro reaedificatione Hierosolymorum, propter Dominum ejusque adventum. Erat quoque primarius Dei scopus in reductione Judaeorum ad patrias illas oras, ut Christus tempore definito apud Judaeos restitutos in terra Canaanis nasceretur. Ergo & hic finis, ob quem LXX. Septimanae decisae erant, statui debet hisce verbis expositus, quae finem decisionis earum continent.
units.tr: 1. Daniel prayed for the rebuilding of Jerusalem on account of the Lord and his coming. God's primary purpose in bringing the Jews back to their ancestral shores was also that Christ should be born at the appointed time among the Jews restored in the land of Canaan. Therefore this end, for which the seventy weeks were marked off, should be stated in these words, which contain the purpose of their determination.

units.la: II. Non officia populi, sed effecta Divina his verbis exponuntur, quod liquet ex natura sermonis Angeli & rei memoratae. Ne omnia percurram; adducere Justitiam aeternam nulli competit, praeter Iehovam Iustitiam nostram. Dicit enim illa phrasis, efficere, ut sit & existat perfectissima Justitia coram Deo. Ipse Vir Clar. non potuit sibi temperare, quin obsignationem visionis & Prophetiæ ad Deum referat quoque. III. Quod maxime attendi velim, non proponuntur hæc effecta, ad claudendum prævaricationem, ut finis rei, id est, temporis & longanimitatis exhibendæ, quæ ad resipiscentiam ducit; sed ut finis Dei decernentis. Si rem presfius consideremus, apparet contineri hoc versu declarationem aterni decreti divini, quoad finem à Deo intentum. Non enim promittitur modo gratia Dei ergà populum, ejusque tempus, sed decretum Dei enarratur de tempore præcisò. Ut sensus sit; decrevit Deus vobis dare tantum temporis, hac intentione, ut fiat certò, quod sequitur, occlusio peccati &c. At finis intentus à Deo in decreto suo semper effectum sortiri debet. Ergò cum populi Judaici incredulitas & impietas sub Templo secundo, præsertim adversus Christum, monstrata constet, eaque severè, juxta hanc prædictionem Danielis, à Deo punita sit; sequitur, si præscriptorum officiorum executio sit finis intentus à Deo decernente, Deum suo fine excidisse, quoniam populus conditionem non implevit. Quod injuriosum Deo ac indecens est. Unde & imprudenter à Viro summo dictum arbitror, stare decisionem divinam, nisi prescripta hæc officia fecerit populus.
units.tr: II. These words set forth not the duties of the people but the works of God, as is clear from the nature of the angel's speech and from the matter at hand. To pass over everything else: to bring in everlasting righteousness belongs to no one except Jehovah, our Righteousness. For the phrase "to bring about" means that the most perfect righteousness should exist and stand before God. The Most Illustrious man could not restrain himself from referring "the sealing of vision and prophecy" to God as well. III. What I particularly want noticed is that these effects are not set forth "to close up transgression" as the end of the thing, that is, of the time and of the forbearance to be shown, which leads to repentance; they are set forth as the end of God, who decrees. If we consider the matter more closely, it appears that this verse contains a declaration of the eternal divine decree, as regards the end intended by God. For it is not merely the grace of God toward the people and its time that is promised; the decree of God is set out concerning a precise period. So the sense is: God has decreed to give you this much time, with the intention that what follows, the "shutting up of sin" and so on, should certainly come to pass. But the end intended by God in his decree must always obtain its effect. Therefore, since the unbelief and impiety of the Jewish people under the second Temple, especially against Christ, is evident, and since they were severely punished by God according to this prediction of Daniel, it follows that if the performance of the prescribed duties were the end intended by God in decreeing, God would have failed of his end, because the people did not fulfil the condition. This is injurious to God and unseemly. Hence I think the great man spoke imprudently when he said that the divine decision stands unless the people had performed these prescribed duties.

units.la: XXX. Non lubet plures aliorum atque alienas exegeses corradere, vel sub examen revocare. Proferemus rectius, quod ad hunc locum dicendum esse arbitramur. Ubi primò consideranda veniunt mala auferenda, triplici vocabulo expressa. Primum est פשע / notans ex origine & usu egressionem ex voluntate, præcepto ac potestate superioris, quæ fit plerumque destinatò & contumaciter. vid. 1 Reg. XII. 19. 2 Reg. I. I. VIII, 10. &c. Secundum est חטאת / notans proprie aberrationem à scopo & viâ illuc ducente Jud. XX. 16. & linea recta, à חוט Tertium עון dicit proprie perversitatem, incurvationem, pravitatem præcipuè in cursu, ex qua frequens cæspitatio; conf. Psal. LIX. 5. XLIX. 6. Primum & ultimum sunt singularia, medium plurale. In quo non puto esse fundamentum distinctionis, quam heic facit Celeb. Coccejus, qui פשע ad defectionem Judæorum à Rege suo, חטאות ad peccata gentilium multifaria, עון ad pravitatem fidelibus adhærescentem, trahit; cum verius primum & ultimum, in singulari posita, collectivè ἐκτιvè sumenda sint. Missis aliis distinctionibus, quas quidam heic faciunt, notamus, quod in sacris, quando omnia omnis generis peccata, quorum infinita mole obrutum est humanum genus, exprimere Spiritus Sanctus constituit, hæc tria vocabula, fœdissimam peccati naturam sua significatione declarantia, frequenter juncta adhibeantur. Vide Exod. xxxiv. 7. Pf. xxxii. 1. 2. & imprimis Levit. xvi. 21. ubi omnia Israelis peccata, quæ confiteri atque hirco emissario imponere ad expiationem debebat sacerdos, tribus hisce vocabulis exprimuntur.
units.tr: XXX. I do not wish to gather together more of the interpretations of others, and of outsiders, or to bring them under examination. We will set out what we judge should rightly be said about this passage. Here we must first consider the evils to be removed, expressed by three words. The first is פשע [pesha], which denotes, from its origin and usage, a departure from the will, command and authority of a superior, usually done deliberately and stubbornly. See 1 Kings 12:19; 2 Kings 1:1; 8:10, etc. The second is חטאת [chatta'th], which properly denotes straying from the goal and from the road leading to it, Judges 20:16, and from the straight line, from חוט. The third, עון ['avon], properly denotes perversity, bending, depravity, especially in running, from which comes frequent stumbling; compare Psalm 59:5; 49:6. The first and last are singular, the middle one plural. I do not think there is any basis for the distinction that the famous Coccejus makes here, who refers פשע to the defection of the Jews from their King, חטאות to the many sins of the Gentiles, and עון to the depravity that clings to believers; for more truly the first and last, being in the singular, should be taken collectively. Setting aside other distinctions that some make here, we note that in the sacred books, when the Holy Spirit has resolved to express all sins of every kind, by which the human race is overwhelmed in an infinite mass, these three words, which declare the most foul nature of sin by their meaning, are frequently used together. See Exodus 34:7; Psalm 32:1, 2, and above all Leviticus 16:21, where all the sins of Israel, which the priest was to confess and lay upon the scapegoat for atonement, are expressed by these three words.

units.la: Et imponet Aharon ambas manus suas capiti hirci vivi, & confitebitur super ipsum אֶת־כָּל־עֲוֺנֹת omnes iniquitates filiorum Israel וְאֶת־כָּל־פִּשְׁעֵיהֶם & omnes defectiones eorum, לְכָל־חַטֹּאתָם cum quibuscunque peccatis eorum, & imponet illa capiti ipsius hirci, & emittet eum per hominem commodum in desertum. Non erit præter rationem, si statuamus, huc digitum intendisse Angelum. Antea observavimus, inter rationes, ob quas tempus hoc decisum per שמטות annosque Sabbaticos numeret, esse etiam hanc, quod in eorum fine Christus effecturus esset expiationem omnium peccatorum veram & consummatam. Quæ observatio fundatur in eo, quod LXX. שמטות /si rite numerentur, desinant in anno Jubileo, & quod hujus promulgati initium sit dies Cippurim. Preterea numerabis tibi septem septimanas annorum, septem annos septem vicibus, ita tempus septem septimanarum annorum sint tibi quadraginta novem anni. Tunc facies, ut ubique personet clangor tubæ mense septimo, die decimo ejus mensis; die expiationum facite, ut personet tuba in tota terra vestra. Ut sanctificetis annum quinquagesimum &c. Levit. xxv. 8. 9. 10. Quia ergo in fine hujus temporis decreti talia miseris mortalibus per Christum erant adferenda beneficia spiritualia, quæ analogiam habebant cum iis, quæ obtingebant Israeli in anno Jubileo, & die Expiationis, ejus initio, quæque spiritualium horum umbræ & figuræ erant; ideo Angelus LXX. Hebdomadas annorum nominat, atque de defectionibus, peccatis, iniquitatibus, tunc vere per Christum expiandis, uti olim typice, edisserit. Ex qua observatione sequitur, non tantum, quod peccata non omnium, sed electi Israelis solius indigitentur, sed etiam, quod ea, non maculæ aut vitii insiti, sed reatus respectu heic intelligi debeant. Eo nomimine enim peccata Israelis olim hirco imposita fuêre, & per ipsum facramentaliter ablata.
units.tr: "And Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the living goat and confess over him all the iniquities [אֶת־כָּל־עֲוֺנֹת] of the children of Israel, and all their transgressions [וְאֶת־כָּל־פִּשְׁעֵיהֶם], and all their sins [לְכָל־חַטֹּאתָם], and he shall put them upon the head of the goat and send him away into the wilderness by the hand of a fit man." It would not be out of place to suppose that the angel had this passage in view. Earlier we observed that among the reasons why this time is numbered by the sabbatical years and jubilees (שמטות), this is also one: that at their end Christ would effect the true and complete expiation of all sins. This observation rests on the fact that the seventy sabbatical periods, if rightly counted, end in the Jubilee year, and that the beginning of its proclamation is the Day of Atonement. "Moreover you shall number seven sabbaths of years for yourself, seven times seven years, so that the time of the seven sabbaths of years shall be to you forty-nine years. Then you shall cause the trumpet to sound everywhere in the seventh month, on the tenth day of that month; on the Day of Atonement you shall cause the trumpet to sound throughout all your land. And you shall hallow the fiftieth year," etc. Leviticus 25:8–10. Therefore, since at the end of this decreed time such spiritual benefits were to be brought to wretched mortals through Christ, benefits which had an analogy with those that came to Israel in the Jubilee year and on the Day of Atonement at its beginning, and which were the shadows and figures of these spiritual goods, the angel names the seventy weeks of years and sets forth the defections, sins and iniquities that were then truly to be expiated through Christ, as once they were expiated typically. From this observation it follows not only that the sins of not all men, but of the elect Israel alone, are pointed out, but also that these sins are to be understood here not as a stain or inborn vice but as guilt. For it was in this sense that the sins of Israel were once laid upon the goat and by it sacramentally removed.

units.la: XXXI. Ablationis porro modum egregiè declarat Angelus, triplici itidem verbo. Primum est כלא. Multi volunt ob vicissitudinem literarum אהוי / literam א pro ה esse positam, ut radix ut כלה notione consummandi, consumendi. V. V. habet ut consummetur prævaricatio. Expressum id est ex Græca versione, quæ habet ἕως ἂν συντελεσθῆναι ἁμαρτίαν. Apud Theodoretum legitur ἑως ἂν πεπλαισθῆναι τὸ ἀπόπτωμα καὶ ἂν τελεσθῆναι ἁμαρτίαν. Prius illud modo apud Tertullianum reperitur; Quoad usque inveteretur delictum. Patet, autores harum versionum כלא pro כלה sumsisse, quod verbum cum consummare, finem imponere, consumere etiam, & facere ut res disparcat, notet, hinc Græci לכלא per τελεσθῆναι & πεπλαισθῆναι expresserunt. Utramque hanc vocem cum legamus apud Theodoretum, miramur magis ipsius expositionem, quam cum Eusebio & Chrysostomo communem habet, & juxta quam consummatio & antiquatio peccati notaret augmentum summum & supremum impietatis culmen, ad quod, per crucifixionem Christi, Judæi increduli assurgerent. Certe ita non antiquatum est peccatum, sed vires & robur majus nactum; quod autem inveterascit, indies magis deficit & est ἐσχύς ἀφανισμός. Ne dicam de contextu sequenti, ubi per vocabula חחכם & כפר / non incrementum sed abolitio peccati significatur. Rectius itaque alii, per consummationem & antiquationem peccati, hujus deletionem & abolitionem gratiosam intelligunt. XXXII. Verum absque necessitate de permutatione literæ ה in א hic cogitant, cum vox כלא / retenta litera א / sua significatione optimum sensum fundat. Scilicet notat כלא proprie claudere 1 Sam. VI. 10. Jer. XXXII. 2. 3. Ps. LXXXVIII. 9. &c. Unde כלא cum duobus Segol, & כליא carcer, & מכלא ovile, caula, cui pecudes includuntur. Hinc & Græcum κλείω claudo, κλεὶς clavis &c. Retinemus nos hunc sensum claudendi, qui primus & proprius & hic ἐμφατικώτερος est, uti ex sequenti nostra exegesi amplius patebit. Sicuti jam id quod clauditur, à conspectu abscondistur, & ne noceat inhibetur, ita defectionem claudendam dicit Angelus, quod à conspectu Dei Judicis removeretur, ne videret & puniret eam, atque ita coerceretur, ut peccatorem resipiscentem accusare, debiti postulare, eumque condemnare coram tribunali Dei amplius non posset.
units.tr: XXXI. The angel declares the manner of removal in a particularly striking way, again by a threefold word. The first is כלא [kala]. Many think that, because of the interchange of the letters ה and א, the letter א has been put for ה, so that the root is כלה, meaning "to finish" or "to consume". The Vulgate has "until transgression be consummated." This is expressed from the Greek version, which has "until sin be completed" [ἕως ἂν συντελεσθῆναι ἁμαρτίαν]. In Theodoret it is read "until the apostasy be moulded and sin be finished" [ἑως ἂν πεπλαισθῆναι τὸ ἀπόπτωμα καὶ ἂν τελεσθῆναι ἁμαρτίαν]. The former reading occurs only in Tertullian: "until the offence grows old." It is clear that the authors of these versions took כלא for כלה, which verb, meaning to complete, to put an end to, and also to consume and bring a thing to nothing, is why the Greeks rendered לכלא by τελεσθῆναι and πεπλαισθῆναι. Although we read both words in Theodoret, we are more struck by his exposition, which he shares with Eusebius and Chrysostom, and according to which the "consummation and antiquation" of sin would signify the greatest increase and the supreme height of impiety, to which the unbelieving Jews would rise through the crucifixion of Christ. Certainly sin is not thus "antiquated" but has acquired greater strength and vigour; for what grows old fades day by day, and is a withering of strength [ἐσχύς ἀφανισμός]. Not to mention the following context, where by the words "to finish transgression" and "to seal up sin" not an increase but an abolition of sin is signified. More correctly, therefore, others understand by the consummation and antiquation of sin its gracious deletion and abolition. XXXII. But without any necessity they think here of an exchange of the letter ה for א, since the word כלא, retaining the letter א, yields the best sense by its own meaning. Namely, כלא properly means "to shut up": 1 Samuel 6:10; Jeremiah 32:2, 3; Psalm 88:9, etc. Whence כלא with two segols, and כליא "a prison," and מכלא "a fold, a pen," in which flocks are shut up. Hence also the Greek κλείω "I shut," κλεὶς "a key," etc. We retain this sense of "shutting up," which is the first and proper one and here the more emphatic, as will become clearer from our exegesis that follows. Just as what is shut up is hidden from sight and prevented from doing harm, so the angel says that the defection is to be "shut up," because it would be removed from the sight of God the Judge, so that he would not see it and punish it, and it would be so restrained that it could no longer accuse the penitent sinner, demand the debt, and condemn him before the tribunal of God.

units.la: XXXIII. Non modo claudendam defectionem, sed & inviolabili sigillo obsignanda peccata, ut nunquam erumpere queant, porro declarat Deus, altero verbo לחחם. Juxta Masorethas Keri hic est להחם ad finiendum, absolvendum, consumendum &c. Sequuntur alii τὸ Keri, alii τὸ Cetif retinent. Absque ullo de boni sensus jactura periculo alterutrum eligi potest. Utrumque enim τὸ Keri & τὸ Cetif à Sp. Sancto profectum, ac æque authenticum, cum quibusdam, non dicerem. Cum autem τὸ Cetif non facile deserendum sit, (voce in textu retenta, ex codicum vetustate, vel plurium consensu, in quibus reperiebatur,) nisi vel forma Grammatica plane fit aliena, vel sensus parum commodus inde emersurus evidenter deprehendatur; tutissimum judicamus illud heic retinere, quia sensus optimus inde emergit, nec ratio Grammatica validè obstat. Regulariter quidem deberet media radicalis ח in לחַמְּם esse dagessata cum praecedente vocali brevi patach. Sed non praeter consuetudinem est, in conjugationibus dagessatis, indagessabilium instar compensationem quandoque sumere non modo ק & ג sed & ח in הַחַל illusit Gen. xxxi. 7. & הָחַל illudere Exod. viii. 25. pro הַחַל & הָחַל: Atque hoc modo legendum esse non dubitarunt Graeci, vertentes, ξσφεγγίσωι. Quam lectionem etiam secutus est Tertullianus, quoad usque signentur peccata. Et apposite satis obsignatio peccatorum eorum occlusioni jungitur, quia illud, quod firmiter clausum volumus, obsignare solemus Dan. vi. 18. Matth. xxvii. 66. Hinc & inter alias & multas vocis hujus significationes ea etiam obtinet, qua notat aliquid quasi valida occlusione abscondere & occultare ab aliorum conspectu Dan. xii. 4. 2. Job xxxvii. 7. Apoc. xxii. 10. Quo sensu & heic venit, notans adeo peccatorum omnium absconsionem validam, non ut memoriam eorum retineat, ac diligenter asservet ea Deus, ne ullum elabatur impunitum, conf. Job. xiv. 7. sed ut eorum prorsus oblivisccatur, ut pereant, nec in rationes Dei veniant in aeternum, ut eorum intuitu peccatorem condemnet; & ut suppressa, subacta, ac in maris profundifunditates abjecta, Mich. vii. 19. vi accusandi & condemnandi peccatorem penitus destituantur.
units.tr: XXXIII. God further declares that sins must not only be shut up but also sealed with an inviolable seal, so that they can never break out. He does so with another word, לחתם [lehatem]. According to the Masoretes, the Keri here is להחם [lehahem], meaning to finish, to complete, to consume, and so on. Some follow the Keri, others keep the Ketiv. Either may be chosen without any risk to the good sense. I would not, however, say with some that both the Keri and the Ketiv proceeded from the Holy Spirit and are equally authentic. Since the Ketiv should not be lightly abandoned (the word having been kept in the text because of the antiquity of the manuscripts or the agreement of the several in which it is found), we judge it safest to retain it here, unless either the grammatical form is plainly out of place or a less suitable sense clearly emerges from it. The best sense emerges from it, and the grammatical objection does not seriously stand in the way. Strictly speaking, the middle radical ח in לַחְתֵּם ought to be doubled after the preceding short vowel patach. But in doubled conjugations it is not unusual for ק and ג, and sometimes also ח, to take the place of letters that cannot be doubled, as in Gen. 31:7 and Exod. 8:25, where הַחַל and הָחַל stand for the forms with the doubling. The Greeks did not hesitate to read it in this way, translating it [ἐσφραγίσωι]. Tertullian also followed this reading, "until sins are sealed." And the sealing of sins is quite fittingly joined to their closing, because we usually seal what we want to keep firmly shut (Dan. 6:18; Matt. 27:66). Hence, among the many meanings of this word, there is also the one that denotes hiding and concealing something from the sight of others by a strong kind of closure (Dan. 12:4; Job 37:7; Rev. 22:10). In this sense it occurs here too, denoting so firm a concealment of all sins. God does this not so that he keeps their memory and carefully preserves them, lest any escape unpunished (cf.
