units.la: Nempe locus ille secretissimus erat Thronus Dei Jer. XVII. 12. qui habitabat ibi inter Cherubim Ps. LXXX. 2. 2. Sam. VI. 2. & præsentiam suam symbolo Nubis, uti volunt plurimi ex Levit. XVI. 2. vel Arca simpliciter, ut alii, ex qua responsa dabat Exod. XXV. 22. indicabat. Ita Christi humana natura est habitaculum Filii Dei, in qua habitat plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter Coll. II. 9. per veram arctissimam & immutabilem duarum naturarum unionem, quæ non nisi levi umbra adumbrata est Dei in habitatione in Sanctuario. Pertinet & huc; Deus manifestatus est in carne 1. Tim. III. 6. Olim Deus in Sanctuario habitans se occultavit, & in caligine habitavit; sed quando Sermo caro factus est, atque in ea ἐσκήνωσε inter homines, tum manifestatus est Deus in carne, ut in habitaculo suo omnium oculis exposito. Præterea Sanctum Sanctorum erat דביר oraculi sedes, unde Deus responsa dabat petentibus, voluntatemque suam revelabat gratiosè Exod. XXV. 22. Ibi etiam faciem Dei quærere debebant 1. Reg. VIII. 33. 34. atque illuc corpus convertere & manus extendere in precibus Ps. V. 8. XXVIII. 2. 1. Reg. VIII. 48. Dan. VI. 11. Sic per filium nos alloquitur Deus Heb. 1. 1. sic in Christo facies Dei quærenda precibus Joh. XIV. & sic omnis cultus noster Deo exhibendus per fidem in Christum & oculis fidei jugiter ad eum conversis, si gratus ipsi futurus sit Heb. XI. 6. sic tandem unice Deum propitium in Christo invenire possumus 2. Cor. V. 19. 1. Joh. 1. 1. Denique ut concludam in Sancto Sanctorum plurima Levitici cultus mymysteria recondita erant. Ibi Arca, Propiatorium, Cherubim, Manna, Virga Aaronis & in horum omnium recta intelligentia maxima sita erat sapientia & consolatio, Ita in Christo multa sunt mysteria. Quicquid Arca, Manna, Virga Aaronis, &c. praefigurabant, in ipso veritatem habet; unde in ejus cognitione est summa sapientia laetitia consolatio, imo vita aeterna Ioh. xvii. 3. 1. Cor. ii. 2. Hinc חכמה Sapientia summa audit objective etiam Prov. ix. 1. Putem huc respexisse Paulum, quando de Christo dicit, ἐν ᾧ εἰσι πάντες οἱ θησαυροὶ τῆς γνώσεως ἀπόκρυφοι. In quo sunt omnes Thesauri sapientiae ac cognitionis absconditi.
units.tr: For that most secret place was the throne of God, Jer. XVII. 12., who dwelt there between the cherubim, Ps. LXXX. 2.; 2 Sam. VI. 2., and showed his presence by the symbol of a cloud, as most hold, from Lev. XVI. 2., or simply by the ark, as others say, from which he gave answers, Exod. XXV. 22. So the human nature of Christ is the dwelling of the Son of God, in which the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily, Col. II. 9., through the true, most close and unchangeable union of two natures, which was only faintly foreshadowed by the dwelling of God in the sanctuary. This also belongs here: God was manifested in the flesh, 1 Tim. III. 16. Formerly God, dwelling in the sanctuary, hid himself and dwelt in darkness; but when the Word became flesh and tabernacled among men, then God was manifested in the flesh, as in his dwelling set open to the eyes of all. Moreover, the Holy of Holies was the seat of the oracle [דביר], whence God gave answers to those who asked and graciously revealed his will, Exod. XXV. 22. There they were to seek the face of God, 1 Kings VIII. 33, 34., and there to turn their body and stretch out their hands in prayers, Ps. V. 8.; XXVIII. 2.; 1 Kings VIII. 48.; Dan. VI. 11. So God speaks to us through the Son, Heb. I. 1.; so in Christ the face of God is to be sought by prayer, John XIV.; and so all our worship to be offered to God is through faith in Christ, with the eyes of faith continually turned towards him, if it is to be pleasing to him, Heb. XI. 6.; and so at last we can find God propitious only in Christ, 2 Cor. V. 19.; 1 John I. 1. Finally, to sum up, the many mysteries of the Levitical worship were hidden in the Holy of Holies. There were the ark, the mercy seat, the cherubim, the manna, the rod of Aaron; and in the right understanding of all of these lay the greatest wisdom and consolation. So in Christ there are many mysteries. Whatever the ark, the manna, the rod of Aaron, etc. foreshadowed, has its truth in him; hence in the knowledge of him is the highest wisdom, joy and consolation, indeed eternal life, John XVII. 3.; 1 Cor. II. 2. Hence the highest wisdom [חכמה] is also heard objectively, Prov. IX. 1. I think Paul had this in view when he says of Christ: in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge [ἐν ᾧ εἰσι πάντες οἱ θησαυροὶ τῆς γνώσεως ἀπόκρυφοι].

units.la: L. Hanc Sanctitatem Sanctitatum tandem Ungendam dicit Angelus. Divina ordinatione ungebantur olim res, vel personae, prae caeteris eximiae, ac specialem relationem ad Deum habentes Exod. xxx. 26. 27. 30. Levit. viii. 12. 1. Sam. ix. 16. x. 1. xv. 12. 13. 1. Reg. xix. 15. 16. Erat tum Unctio in iis signum ac publica declaratio divinae electionis ad singularem Dei inhabitationem, vel ad munus praeclarum, & donorum Spiritus, ad id rite & alacriter obeundum conferendorum. Frequentissime Mediator promissus nomine Uncti proponitur, ac unctio ei tribuitur 1. Sam. ii. 2. xlv. 8. Ies. lxi. 1. Dan. ix. 25. 26. &c. Intelligitur autem ea non corporalis, sed spiritualis. Nempe Unctus Mediator dictus, quia persona excellentissima foret, munus dignissimum triplex gereret, ad haec ab aeterno constitutus Prov. viii. 23. ac ut talis in tempore publice declarandus, donaque Spiritus, ob multiplicem convenientiam per oleum merito repraesentata, largissima manu effusa, acciperet. Quod cuncta haec nomine Unctionis vel Uncti Mediatori tributo comprehendi possint, liquet ex collatione locorum, in quibus speciali relatione ad res vel personas unctas, sive Prophetas Ies. lxi. 1. sive Reges Ps. ii. 6. &c. ipsi tribuitur unctio. Qualem specialem respectum etiam heic reperiunt multi. Alii ad munus Sacerdotale. Ita Cloppenburg. De sacerdotali unctione est oraculum Ps. cx. 4. &c. Nec non Dan. ix. de ungendo Sancto Sanctorum vers. 24. &c. vid. Disput. Select. xvii. §. xix. Quando Unctio heic denotabit declarationem Mediatoris, ut consummati Sacerdotis, per opera sacerdotalia, occlusionem & expiationem peccatorum, passionibus obedientia junctis perficiendam, conf. Heb. 11. 10. Alii ad munus Regium respiciunt; est enim unctus Princeps, quando rursus unctio hæc denotat declarationem Mediatoris, ut gloriosissimi Regis, per collocationem ad dextram Patris, postquam in hisce terris peccata expiasset, ut laboris debitam mercedem, atque ad beneficiorum acquisitorum applicationem certam. Si autem sub typo Sancti Sanctorum Christum repræsentatum velimus, ad hujus olim mandatam unctionem Exod. xxx. 26. respectum esse cogitare possumus. Scilicet illa erat delaratio, singularis eminentia loci, à Deo electi in habitaculum, ac in sedem cultus publici. Præterea erat symbolum donorum Spiritus, quibus corpus omnium harum umbrarum inungi debet, si sanguine sacrificiali & efficacia applicationis efficeret, ut Dei Tabernaculum apud homines, in gratia & in gloria, constituatur, & illi vicissim apud Deum habitarent cum fide & amore ejus. Huc ergo alludens Spiritus, duo de Filio Dei proponit. 1. Fore Illum personam dignissimam, & à communi hominum sorte longissimè separatam, in Naturis, Muneribus, Statu &c. & verum Sanctuarium, in quo Deus se ergà peccatorem electum unicè exhibet gratiosum, atque ut tale declarandum coram omnium oculis. 11. Fore ungendum oleo Spiritus uberrimè, ut promereretur Dei gratiam erga homines peccatores, immaculato ac voluntario sui ipsius sacrificio, atque efficeret per Spiritum, ut homines, hostes Dei, per fidem veritatis & amorem sanctitatis ad ipsum ducerentur; & sic unà habitarent simul. Hæc res implementum sortita est in Jesu Nazareno. Declaratus is est longe supra omnes præstantissimus, non tantum in Naturis, ut Filius Dei, voce cœlesti Matth. iii. 17. xvii. 5. operibus Deo propriis Act. x. 38. nativitate miraculosa Luc. i. 32. resurrectione ex mortuis Rom. i. 3. &c. sed & in Muneribus; sic verba & facta eximium Prophetam; Stella, Magi, Angeli, opera, &c. potentissimum Regem; animi & corporis cum plenissima obedientiâ junctæ passiones, præfiguratum, promissumque diu, nunc consummatum Sacerdotem exhibuerunt. Donis Spiritus etiam uberrimè perfusus est Joh. iii. 34. Jes. xi. 1. 2. in nativitate & ætatis progressu Luc. ii. 52. magis in Baptismo Matth. iii. 16. maximè autem post adscensionem in cœlum, quando dona Spiritus accepit effundenda largiter in corpus my-sticum Psal. LXVIII. 19. XLV. 8. Act. IV. 27. &c.
units.tr: LX. Lastly, the angel says that this Holy of Holies is to be anointed. By divine appointment, things or persons that were outstanding above others and had a special relation to God were anointed in former times, Exod. XXX. 26, 27, 30.; Lev. VIII. 12.; 1 Sam. IX. 16.; X. 1.; XV. 12, 13.; 1 Kings XIX. 15, 16. The anointing was then a sign and public declaration of divine election, either to a singular indwelling of God or to an excellent office, and to the bestowal of gifts of the Spirit for discharging it rightly and readily. Very often the promised Mediator is presented under the name of Anointed, and anointing is ascribed to him, 1 Sam. II. 2.; Ps. XLV. 8.; Isa. LXI. 1.; Dan. IX. 25, 26, etc. It is understood, however, not as a bodily but as a spiritual anointing. For the Mediator is called Anointed, because he would be a most excellent person, would bear a threefold most worthy office, was appointed to these things from eternity, Prov. VIII. 23, and, as such, was to be publicly declared in time, and to receive, poured out with a most lavish hand, the gifts of the Spirit, rightly represented by oil because of its many points of fitness. That all these things can be included under the name Anointing or Anointed ascribed to the Mediator is clear from a comparison of passages in which anointing is ascribed to a person or thing in a special relation to the anointed, whether to Prophets, Isa. LXI. 1., or to Kings, Ps. II. 6, etc. Many find such a special reference also here. Others look to the priestly office. Thus Cloppenburg: "There is an oracle concerning priestly anointing, Ps. CX. 4, etc. Nor is there Dan. IX, concerning anointing the Holy of Holies, verse 24, etc.; see Disput. Select. XVII, §XIX." When the anointing here denotes the declaration of the Mediator as the consummated priest, through priestly acts, the expiation and atonement of sins, to be accomplished through sufferings joined with obedience, compare Heb. II. 10. Others look to the kingly office; for he is the anointed Prince, when again this anointing denotes the declaration of the Mediator as the most glorious King, by his placement at the right hand of the Father, after he had expiated sins in these lands, as the due reward of his labour, and as a sure application of the benefits acquired. If, however, we want Christ to be represented under the type of the Holy of Holies, we may consider that there is a reference to the anointing commanded of old, Exod. XXX. 26. Clearly that anointing was a declaration of the singular eminence of the place, chosen by God as his dwelling and as the seat of public worship. Moreover, it was a symbol of the gifts of the Spirit, with which the body of all these shadows must be anointed, if by sacrificial blood and the efficacy of application it should bring about that God's tabernacle is established among men, in grace and in glory, and they in turn dwell with him in faith and love. Alluding to this, the Spirit sets forth two things about the Son of God. First, that he will be a most worthy person, far removed from the common lot of men in his natures, offices, state, etc., and a true Sanctuary in which God uniquely shows himself gracious towards the elect sinner, and to be declared as such before the eyes of all. Second, that he will be anointed most richly with the oil of the Spirit, so that by his immaculate and voluntary self-sacrifice he might merit God's grace towards sinful men, and so effect, through the Spirit, that men, enemies of God, are led to him through faith in the truth and love of holiness, and thus dwell with him together. This thing has been fulfilled in Jesus of Nazareth. He has been declared far above all most excellent: not only in his natures, as the Son of God, by the heavenly voice, Matt. III. 17; XVII. 5; by works proper to God, Acts X. 38; by his miraculous birth, Luke I. 32; by his resurrection from the dead, Rom. I. 3, etc.; but also in his offices: thus words and deeds have exhibited him as an outstanding Prophet, the Star, the Magi, the angels, his works, etc. as a most powerful King, and as the Priest long foreshadowed and promised, now consummated, whose sufferings were joined with the most complete obedience of soul and body. He was also most richly endowed with the gifts of the Spirit, John III. 34; Isa. XI. 1, 2, in his birth and in the progress of his age, Luke II. 52; more at his baptism, Matt. III. 16; but most of all after his ascension into heaven, when he received the gifts of the Spirit to pour out abundantly upon his mystical body, Ps. LXVIII. 19; XLV. 8; Acts II. 33, etc.

units.la: LXI. Hæc sunt illa Messiæ beneficia, quæ intra LXX. Septimanarum spatium, eventura erant.
units.tr: LXI. These are the benefits of the Messiah that were to come within the space of the seventy weeks.

units.la: Non est verò ut multùm nos cruciemus in enodandis difficultatibus, quas heic injicit Chronologia. Nam quod ad Judæos attinet, satis constat, Septimanas has dudum esse elapsas, ac consequenter Messiam venisse, & xpiationem peccatorum peregisse, Urbis excidio, de quo in sequentibus etiam agitur, comprobatam. Nec Dei immutabile decretum, absoluta prorsus promissio, ac finis adventus Messiæ, qui est peccatorum expiatio, patiuntur, ut exceptioni Judaicæ, de dilata impletione promissi hujus ob peccata populi, aures præbeamus modò. Uti neque cavillis eorum, de dissensu Christianorum, in assignando principio, & fine Septimanarum, enumerandisque annis interjectis, diu immorari opus est.
units.tr: We need not torment ourselves much in untangling the chronological difficulties raised here. As far as the Jews are concerned, it is quite clear that these weeks have long since run out, and consequently that the Messiah has come and has made expiation for sins, as the destruction of the City, which is also discussed below, confirms. Nor do the immutable decree of God and the absolute promise, and the purpose of the Messiah's coming, which is the expiation of sins, allow us to lend an ear to the Jewish objection that the fulfilment of this promise was deferred because of the people's sins. Nor is there any need to linger over the quibbles of Christians who disagree about the starting point and end of the weeks and the counting of the intervening years.

units.la: Paucis modò dicimus, a reductione populi ex Edicto Cyri, usque ad mortem Christi, vulgò à Chronologis plures paulò annos numerari, quam 490. Omnes fatentectur, juxta Josephum, mortem Alexandri M. contigisse Olymp. CXIV. Christi verò statuitur vulgò Olymp. CCII. ann. vel 4. Patet inde, ad anno mortis Alexandri M. si primus is dicatur Olymp. CXIV. usque ad annum mortis Christi, si quartus Olymp. CCII. fuerit, fluxisse fere 354. annos. Quibus addantur 67 Alexandri, qui ei adscribuntur, inde ab Imperio Orbis post cœsum Darium, resultantinde 361. vel 362. Quod si jam clare posset hypothesis Bronglone de CXXX. annis Monarchiæ Persicæ, res satis expedita foret.
units.tr: We need only say briefly that from the return of the people under the edict of Cyrus to the death of Christ, the chronologers commonly count a few more than 490 years. All agree, following Josephus, that the death of Alexander the Great fell in Olympiad 114. The birth of Christ, however, is commonly placed in Olympiad 202, year or 4. It is clear from this that, if the death of Alexander the Great is taken as the first year of Olympiad 114 and the year of Christ's death as the fourth year of Olympiad 202, there elapsed from the one to the other almost 354 years. To these must be added the 67 years that are assigned to Alexander from the beginning of his rule of the world after the defeat of Darius, which gives a total of 361 or 362. If the hypothesis of Brongnoli about the 130 years of the Persian monarchy could now be clearly established, the matter would be fairly resolved.

units.la: Verum Monarchicam Persicam minimùm CC. annos duraffe, graves & probati historici jure veteres, sive recentes asserunt. Persas non multum ultra 200 annos in rerum fastigio permannisse, author est Dionys. Halicarn. Porro quod Cyrus Olymp. 55. an. 1 regnare, in Persidè cæperit uno ore Veteres, uti Julius Africanus, laudatus ab Eusebio, scriptum reliquit. Ad Olymp. autem CXII. annum quemcunque, in quo finem Persica Monarchia, sub Dario Codomanno, accepit, à primo LV. ducenti & triginta plus minus anni intercesserunt; consequenter ab initio Monarchiæ Cyri, usque ad mortem Darii Codomanni, non multum ultra, sed tamen ultra 200 anni sunt. Idem patet ex annis singulorum Regum Herodoto, Ctesiæ, Josepho.
units.tr: But the older and recent historians, grave and approved authorities, rightly maintain that the Persian monarchy lasted at least 200 years. The Persians did not remain at the height of power much more than 200 years, is the testimony of Dionysius of Halicarnassus. Furthermore, that Cyrus began to reign over Persia in Olympiad 55, year 1, is stated with one voice by the ancients, as Eusebius reports, quoting Julius Africanus. From the first year of Olympiad 55 to the year of Olympiad 112 in which the Persian monarchy came to an end under Darius Codomannus, roughly 230 years intervened; consequently, from the beginning of Cyrus's monarchy to the death of Darius Codomannus, there are not much more than, but still more than, 200 years. The same is clear from the reigns of the individual kings as given by Herodotus, Ctesias, Josephus.

units.la: obstup sepho, Diodoro Siculo, Clementi Alexandrino, Eusebio &c. licet insigni varietate memoratis, etiam Ptolemæo in Canone. Quid ergo? an dicendum est omnes hos falsos & mendaces esse, utpote Danieli adversos? Ægre id à me impetrarem. Cogitandum itaque est, annon aliqua via reperiri possit conciliandi Danielem cum Chronologia exotica. Recurrit Raimoldus ad Synecdochen, ut numerus minor pro majori, certus pro incerto, rotundus pro non rotundo, & per allusionem ad Lxx. annos captivitatis Lxx. septimanæ annorum modò nominarentur; non præcisè intelligendæ, quia hęc non est historica narratio, sed Prophetica prædictio, in quâ memoriæ levandæ causâ, vel allusione ad typum, numerus certus pro incerto poni potest. coll. Gen. xv. 13. Gal. iii. 17. Sequerer hoc, nisi vox חתך / & divisio septimanarum in partes obstaret. Alii Lxx. Septimanas continere contendunt tempora tantum ædificationis Templi & Civitatis, hujusque ædificatæ inhabitationis, non vero tempora cessationis ab ædificando, quæ verius ad miseriam captivitatis, quam libertatem pertineant. Quorsum referri posse illud עבצוק העתם / Et in angustia temporā, sc. quædam erunt, suspicatur Clar. Coccejus. Quando hoc modo calculos instituit Clar. L'Empereur. Septem septimanæ excurrerunt, id est, tantum temporis variis intervallis impensum est ædificationi Templi, à primo Cyri, usque ad septimum Artaxerxis Mnemonis, scilicet à Cyro ad Xerxem, qui opus Templi impedit, excurrunt anni 46. haud plene tamen; quibus fermè ædificabatur Templum, opere illo simul variis modis impedito. Deinde continuò intermissum est ad annum 2 Darii Nothi, quo resumtum opus ad fastigium perductum est, circa annum illius 6, id est, spatio ad minimum 3. annorum; quos si addas præcedentibus 46, exurgent anni 49, id est septimanæ septem. Post hæc (quæcunque etiam fuerit causa) manus extrema non est adhibita ante 7 Artaxerxis illius, qui Dario Notho successit. Hoc, quantulumcunque fuerit temporis, si addas annis illis primis 46, supplementi loco, quia pleni non fuerunt, justum habebis (additis ut dictum est tribus Darii annis) numerum 49. Ab hoc anno 7 Artaxerxis ad Christi 30. cum non fluxerint Lxii. Septimanæ, seu an. 434, sed 427, qui cum 49. & 7, ultimæ septimanæ, 48 annos solum conficiunt; sciendum est Spir. units.tr: Josephus, Diodorus Siculus, Clement of Alexandria, Eusebius etc., although they differ considerably in what they report, and also Ptolemy in his Canon. What then? Must we say that all these are false and lying, as being opposed to Daniel? I would find it hard to bring myself to that. We must therefore consider whether some way can be found of reconciling Daniel with the foreign chronology. Raimoldus has recourse to synecdoche, so that a smaller number is put for a larger, a certain number for an uncertain one, a round number for one that is not round; and by allusion to the seventy years of the captivity, the seventy weeks of years are only named, not to be understood precisely, because this is not a historical narrative but a prophetic prediction, in which, for the sake of ease of memory or by allusion to a type, a certain number may be put for an uncertain one (compare Gen. 15:13, Gal. 3:17). I would follow this, were it not that the word cut off [חתך] and the division of the weeks into parts stand in the way. Others contend that the seventy weeks comprise only the time of building the Temple and the City and the inhabiting of the city once built, not the time of the cessation from building, which pertains rather to the misery of the captivity than to liberty. Coccejus, the distinguished scholar, suspects that the phrase in straits of the times [עבצוק העתם], that is, and in the straits of the times, could be referred to this. L'Empereur, the distinguished scholar, reckons in this way. Seven weeks ran out, that is, the time spent on building the Temple in various intervals, from the first year of Cyrus to the seventh of Artaxerxes Mnemon: that is, from Cyrus to Xerxes, who hindered the work on the Temple, the years run to 46, though not fully; in these the Temple was nearly built, the work being at the same time hindered in various ways. Then it was interrupted continuously until the second year of Darius Nothus, when the work was resumed and brought to completion, around the sixth year of that king, that is, over a space of at least 3 years; if you add these to the preceding 46, you get 49 years, that is seven weeks. After this, for whatever reason, the finishing touch was not put on until the seventh year of that Artaxerxes who succeeded Darius Nothus. If you add to the first 46 years this period, however short it was, as a supplement, since the years were not full, you will have (adding, as said, the three years of Darius) the proper number of 49. From this seventh year of Artaxerxes to the thirtieth year of Christ, since the sixty-two weeks, that is 434 years, did not run out but only 427, these, together with the 49 and the 7, make the last week only 48 years; it must be noted that the Holy Spirit sometimes in the prophecies...

units.la: H prophetiis de Ecclesiæ calamitatibus, vel de liberatione ex iisdem, respicere ad Israelitarum Exodum ex Ægypto, ideoque in calculo instituendo adhibere annos, quibus assueverant antiquissimi in Ægypto. Anni autem isti habebant 12. menses æquales, tricenis diebus descriptos. Hujusmodi autem menses absque additamento conficiunt annos, qui constant diebus 360. adeoque à nostris solaribus superantur diebus quinque & horis sex, conficientibus in hoc numero annorum 483, annos 7 plus minus, qui addi debent annis illis 483, atque hac ratione conveniet numerus. Vid. L'Empereur in Not. ad Paraph. Jachiad. in Dan. Alii tandem Edictum non unum Regium, aut primum Cyri solum, sed quatuor successive promulgata complexim sumenda censent, utpote ad unum finem tendentia, dum posteriora interpretamenta priorum fuere. Quod eò magis plausibile est, quo minus in uno Edicto v: g: Cyri expresse non reperiatur id omne, quod Angelus dicit de verbo egresso, nempe ilud fore non tantum de reducendo populo, sed & dè reædificandis Hierosolymis; quod posteriùs explicitè quidem non habetur in Edicto Cyri, sed in ultimo Artaxerxis. Quo pacto omnia rectè fluerent, si probari posset, Artaxerxem, sub quo Nehemiah rediit & urbem instaurarit, esse Artaxerxem Longimanum. Anno enim 20 regni permisit Nehemiæ reditum ad restaurandam urbem. Regnavit juxta Ctesiam annos 42. Darius Nothus ann. 19. Artax. Mnemon 43. Ochus 23. Arses 3. Darius Codomamnas 7. quibus additi 6 vel 7 usque ad Alexandri M. mortem resultant anni 485, vel si annum unum Xerxi 11. & Sogdiano adscribere volumus, à 20. Artaxerxis Longimani, usque ad passionem Christi, quam si contigisse dimidio primo, vel mediοseptimanæ dicamus, annos 490 in quarto post passionem anno completos videmus. Verum non est necesse ita determinatè annos ad unum numerare. Satis constat fides Oraculi, etiamsi una aut altera difficultas in annis numerandis remaneat. Hoc pedem figimus. Orantes Deum, ut Judæorum oculos tandem aperire velit, ut videant in Jesu Crucifixo fontem horum beneficiorum ac omnis salutis, ut nos gratos pro tantis beneficiis in sanguine Filii acceptis, continuò in cognitione fide amore Christi progredi, & unctionis ipsius participes faciat hèic in gratia, donec tandem in gloria fructus Justitiæ ejus æternæ in æternum nancisčamur.
units.tr: In prophecies concerning the calamities of the Church, or concerning deliverance from them, the Holy Spirit looks back to the exodus of the Israelites from Egypt, and therefore in making the calculation uses the years to which the most ancient people in Egypt were accustomed. Those years had 12 equal months, each described as thirty days. Such months, without any addition, make years consisting of 360 days, and so they fall short of our solar years by five days and six hours; in this number of 483 years, taking up seven years more or less, which must be added to those 483 years, and in this way the number will agree. See L'Empereur in Notes on the Paraphrase of Jachiades on Daniel. Others finally think that the edict to be taken is not one royal edict, nor only the first of Cyrus, but several promulgated successively taken together, as tending to one end, since the later ones were interpretations of the earlier. This is all the more plausible because in one edict, for example that of Cyrus, there is not expressly found all that the angel says about the word going forth, namely that it would concern not only the return of the people but also the rebuilding of Jerusalem; this is not explicitly found later in the edict of Cyrus, but in the last edict of Artaxerxes. All things would fall into place correctly if it could be proved that the Artaxerxes under whom Nehemiah returned and restored the city was Artaxerxes Longimanus. For in the twentieth year of his reign he permitted Nehemiah's return to restore the city. According to Ctesias he reigned 42 years; Darius Nothus 19; Artaxerxes Mnemon 43; Ochus 23; Arses 3; Darius Codomannus 7; adding to these 6 or 7 years up to the death of Alexander the Great, the years come to 485; or if we wish to assign one year to Xerxes and to Sogdianus, from the twentieth year of Artaxerxes Longimanus to the passion of Christ, which, if we say it took place in the first half or middle of the seventieth week, we find 490 years completed in the fourth year after the passion. But it is not necessary to count the years so precisely to the unit. The truth of the oracle is sufficiently established, even if one or another difficulty about counting the years remains. On this we take our stand. Praying God that he may at last be willing to open the eyes of the Jews, so that they may see in Jesus crucified the source of these benefits and of all salvation; and that he may make us, grateful for such great benefits received in the blood of the Son, continually to progress in the knowledge, faith and love of Christ, and partakers of his anointing here in grace, until at last in glory we may attain in eternity the fruit of his eternal righteousness.
